title: The data and the anecdata on Jev's adoption are shocking. Everyone is adopting it. I think it's a great product, but this is also downstream of the "AI is too expensive/slow" zeitgeist. People are… | Guillermo Rauch | 11 comments
headline: The data and the anecdata on Jev's adoption are shocking.
post_text:
The data and the anecdata on Jev's adoption are shocking. Everyone is adopting it.

I think it's a great product, but this is also downstream of the "AI is too expensive/slow" zeitgeist. People are eager to optimize and put AI in even more places!

top_visible_comments.comment: The adoption rate of Jev is certainly phenomenal. However, it is important to acknowledge the role that models from other providers played in "warming" the audience before Jev was launched. Almost everyone who is using Jev today has used models such as Claude or ChatGPT in the recent past. These models played the role of "user education" before Jev. Nonetheless, the execution speed of Jev is incredible, and I'm excited to see what comes next.
Feels like 2015 when a new React state mgmt lib was introduced every week.  😁

Agreed on the zeitgeist, though I think the two effects have different lifespans.
Replacing expensive calls with cheap ones is a migration. You do it once and you've captured the savings.
The more interesting part is the decisions nobody automated before, because they were too ambiguous for an if/else and too small to justify a model call. That category is much larger than it looks, and it grows as the cost drops.
Worth watching how teams handle oversight there. Nobody reviews a decision that costs a fraction of a cent, so errors only show up in aggregate.
It's brought awareness to a whole world of System One AI.
It doesn't surprise me, Jev replaces 50% of our use cases at a hundredth of the cost and speed.

Tbh people are excited by the idea and also don’t have any idea how to make the best use of a typed decision engine in an AI stack. I’m excited about the downstream from Jev itself because of the applied ontology work that’s gonna fall out of the adoption
Jev is short for Jevon, isn't it :)
Jev is a great idea. Using LLM architecture for dynamic classification. Likely major AI studios will offer a similar API
Jev ❤️

title: I’ve been talking to a lot of companies that’ve struggled to make AI work for their business. One thing is clear: being a remote company is a huge advantage. We’ve moved from AI assistants → AI… | Kieran Flanagan | 52 comments
headline: I’ve been talking to a lot of companies that’ve struggled to make AI work for their business.
post_text:
I’ve been talking to a lot of companies that’ve struggled to make AI work for their business. One thing is clear: being a remote company is a huge advantage. 

We’ve moved from AI assistants → AI agents → AI employees.

AI as an employee needs all your company context, access to all your company tools, and the ability to show up where your team works.

Remote companies have two distinct advantages here:

- everything they do is documented; all of their conversations are recorded: meetings, slacks, emails, etc. Nothing gets lost in those live person interactions.
- those teams are largely working/collaborating in Slack and other apps vs. doing it live in person.

The AI employee can leverage all that rich context to become an incredible asset for the company.

In-person companies need a way to better capture what’s happening away from the screens.

I wouldn’t be surprised to see in the future in-person companies ask employees to wear recording devices to capture meetings, workshops, etc., so nothing is lost. Ask them to collaborate more in messaging apps, in places where that info can be ingested by AI.

At a time when there’s a big shift back to the office, there’s an interesting irony: AI may actually make remote companies better positioned for the future of work.

more_relevant_posts.post_text: With all the talk about coming back to the office and "reducing headcount because of AI", it's ironic that AI might be the thing that gives remote companies more leverage.

AI can automate a lot of work. But there are things AI cannot replace in a remote business environment. It cannot replace: → Judgment — knowing what needs your attention now and what can wait. → Ownership — taking responsibility for making sure a task actually gets completed. → Relationship management — understanding clients, executives, teams, and the human context behind every conversation. → Proactive thinking — spotting a problem before it becomes an expensive problem. → Follow-up — making sure important conversations, decisions, deadlines, and commitments do not disappear into an inbox. → Trust — knowing that someone understands how you work and can protect your time, information, and priorities. → Business context — understanding why a task matters, not simply completing the task. This is where the future of remote work is heading. The competitive advantage isn't choosing between AI or people. It is building systems where AI handles repetitive work and capable people handle judgment, relationships, priorities, and execution. For founders, CEOs, consultants, and small business owners, that combination can mean fewer administrative bottlenecks, better follow-through, and more time spent on decisions that actually grow the business. AI doesn't eliminate the need for great Executive Virtual Assistants. It raises the standard for what a great Executive Virtual Assistant should be. The future belongs to professionals who know how to work with AI, not compete against it.

🚀 NO OFFICE? NO PROBLEM. AI + REMOTE WORK = THE NEW CAREER ADVANTAGE The biggest change happening in the job market isn't simply AI replacing jobs. It is something much more interesting: AI is changing WHERE we work, HOW we work, and WHAT skills companies value. A professional sitting anywhere in the world can now use AI to research faster, automate repetitive tasks, analyse data, create solutions, write documentation, manage projects and solve problems that previously required much larger teams. And that creates a completely new opportunity for professionals. 🤖 The future belongs to AI-enabled professionals You don't necessarily need to become an AI/ML engineer. You can combine AI with your existing experience: 🔹 Project / Program Management + AI 🔹 Business Analysis + AI 🔹 Data & Analytics + AI 🔹 Automation + AI 🔹 Cloud + AI 🔹 Operations + AI 🔹 Digital Transformation + AI 🔹 Customer Experience + AI The winning combination is becoming: Domain Expertise + AI + Automation + Communication 🌍 Why Remote Work Matters Remote work has removed one major limitation: Geography. A talented professional doesn't always need to live next to the company's office. With the right skills, communication, collaboration tools and results-driven mindset, professionals can contribute to teams across cities, countries and time zones. 💡 What should professionals do NOW? Don't wait for the perfect AI course. Start building. 1️⃣ Learn AI tools ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, AI automation platforms and other productivity tools. 2️⃣ Automate one real business problem Don't just learn theory. Build something that saves time or money. 3️⃣ Combine AI with your existing career Your previous experience is an advantage—not something you need to throw away. 4️⃣ Build your LinkedIn presence Show projects, ideas, use cases and measurable outcomes. 5️⃣ Target outcome-based roles Companies don't only need people who know AI. They need people who can use AI to solve business problems. 🔥 My biggest takeaway AI isn't necessarily replacing experienced professionals. But professionals who know how to use AI may increasingly have an advantage over professionals who don't. The future isn't: Human vs AI It is: Human + AI. Learn. Adapt. Automate. Work from anywhere. Create value. 🌎 The office may be optional. Your skills aren't. #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #RemoteJobs #RemoteWork #FutureOfWork #AIJobs #Automation #GenAI #DigitalTransformation #ProjectManagement #ProgramManagement #BusinessAnalysis #DataAnalytics #CloudComputing #CareerGrowth #WorkFromAnywhere #JobSearch #LinkedIn #OpenToWork #Hiring #Recruitment #Technology #Innovation #AIAutomation

🤖 𝐈𝐬 𝐢𝐭 𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐚 𝐛𝐢𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐥𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐀𝐈...? There's a risk we use it to explain everything. That's one of the thoughts this new paper sparked for me. Entry-level hiring has fallen across white-collar work, which is a worrying trend, and people are pointing the finger at generative AI. But this new study by Peter John Lambert and Yannick Schindler suggests things are more complicated. They argue that working from home may also be a factor in explaining the trend. The authors found that companies that offered remote or hybrid roles subsequently reduced the junior share of their hiring relative to otherwise similar firms that didn't offer remote work. And that finding holds even after accounting for differences in AI exposure, WFH exposure and occupation mix. That doesn't mean AI isn't changing entry-level work. But it does suggest the story is more complicated than that. Both remote working and GenAI may be having a compounding effect. And perhaps the bigger question isn't whether AI or WFH is responsible... It's about the transformation of work and jobs more broadly, and what we want work to look like in the future. 🎤 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤? 🔗 Find a link to the article in the comments. 📰 Reference: Lambert, Peter John and Schindler, Yannick, The Broken Ladder: AI, Remote Work, and Early-Career Hiring (May 18, 2026). Available at SSRN: https://buff.ly/yXYWu9J . 🖼️ Image comes from there. 🚴 Enjoy posts like this? 👉 Click 𝐕𝐢𝐞𝐰 𝐦𝐲 𝐛𝐥𝐨𝐠 to get my quarterly roundup.

Remote vs On-site: AI drives the final nail into the coffin of inefficient and outdated corporate structures. A mandated office day is no longer a culture choice. It is a knowledge outage for your AI corporate AI layer. Office and hybrid produce the same artifact: the important part of the work happens where no system can see it. Why: A week ago I finished a six-month project: building and implementing a full-contour corporate AI agent - a human-independent system that can do what no living employee can - be everywhere, process information continuously, and never forget a decision. It ingests three sources — continuously: → all call transcripts → all text communications → the task tracker From that stream it automatically builds and manages the corporate knowledge base, holds operational management context, supports employees, and acts as a decision-making and managing assistant for managers and stakeholders. The results are exceptional. The company finally stopped throwing its own memory in the bin. Which makes the next point obvious. A day of offline "strategic session" is several hours of context that never enters the system. Decisions with no trail. Nuance that dies in the room. Commitments nobody can retrieve next Tuesday — including your own managers. Threats: The window to introduce a change has shrunk. Competitors move in weeks. AI is not a bubble, not a toy technology anymore - it compresses cycles that used to take quarters. A full on-site setup will get you out of business sooner than you think. Hybrid just dresses the same failure in less straightforward manner. If your source of truth is a room, you lose to a company whose source of truth is a system that never sleeps, never forgets, and never needs everyone in the same zip code to decide. For the past 11 years I've worked exclusively remotely. During that time, I've been building teams, developing systems. A co-founded startup built entirely in a remote setting got acquired. Now I've learned how to take these advantages to a truly new level. If that is relevant for you — reach out. #AIStrategy #CEO #DigitalTransformation #Leadership #Innovation

The role of AI in enhancing remote work: Tools that boost productivity. As remote work becomes the norm, AI is proving to be a game changer in keeping us productive and connected. 💻✨ From smart calendars that optimize our schedules to AI-powered chatbots that streamline communication, the right tools can transform our work-from-home experience. Imagine an AI assistant that analyzes your work patterns and suggests the best times for focused tasks, or one that helps manage your email inbox by prioritizing important messages. These tools not only save us time but also enhance our workflow, allowing us to focus on what truly matters. ⏱️📩 In a recent project, I used an AI tool that helped me identify and eliminate distractions, significantly boosting my output. The sense of accomplishment was exhilarating! It’s incredible how these innovations empower us to work more efficiently, no matter where we are. As more companies decide that work once handed to consultants can be handled by AI, Peter Cappelli of The Wharton School says interpersonal skills will increasingly matter. That could spell bad news for those working remotely, Cappelli says. If AI can handle more technical and analytical work, the skills that become more valuable may be distinctly human ones—building relationships, reading a room and working effectively with others. And those can be harder to demonstrate when you're rarely in the room. https://lnkd.in/ep7xWpXg #InterpersonalSkills

Remote teams don’t need more apps — they need AI that connects the apps and takes the busywork off people’s plates. AI can eliminate routine friction for distributed tech teams: smart automation, intelligent scheduling, 24/7 virtual assistants, and automatic status updates reduce interruptions and manual coordination. When AI links disparate systems and automates cross-tool handoffs, teams stop stitching workflows together by hand and start collaborating at a higher level. The biggest shift is from point solutions to orchestration. Instead of bolting single-purpose bots onto silos, prioritize AI that coordinates multi-step processes and manages cognitive load — e.g., timed notifications, concise summaries, and handoff automation that make asynchronous work practical across time zones. What to do now: automate high-frequency admin tasks (scheduling, triage, routine docs), integrate AI at the workflow level to avoid new silos, and evaluate enterprise tools that focus on team-level output and orchestration rather than only individual convenience. Main takeaway: AI-augmented workflows reduce administrative load, enable better asynchronous collaboration, and increase team output when designed to orchestrate end-to-end processes. Which routine task would you automate first to give your team more focus for high-value work?

title: David's Bridal AI-powered wedding planning experience | Mike Kaput posted on the topic | LinkedIn
headline: How can AI reinvent a 76-year-old brand?
post_text:
How can AI reinvent a 76-year-old brand?
You might be surprised:

David’s Bridal is using AI to go from helping brides find a dress to helping you plan an entire wedding…

President Elina Vilk and Head of Product Mike Bal walked me through how the storied brand built an AI-powered end-to-end wedding planning experience from the ground up.

Couples can use it to handle 100s of wedding planning tasks and get guidance on what needs their attention most at each stage of the process.

As they make decisions, it remembers their preferences and adjusts its recommendations.

One detail I loved: If you need to find, say, another $1,000 in your budget, it can suggest cuts based on what you’ve said already matters most to you.)

We cover this and much, much more in the latest episode of The Artificial Intelligence Show as part of our AI Transformations series presented by Google Cloud 👇

title: I used to think freedom was something you earned after working hard enough. Now I think it’s something you design into the business. The old version of entrepreneurship… | Matt Gray | 45 comments
headline: I used to think freedom was something you earned after working hard enough.
post_text:
I used to think freedom was something you earned after working hard enough.

Now I think it’s something you design into the business.

The old version of entrepreneurship glorified:

Stress.

Sleepless nights.

A packed calendar.

Being needed for everything.

I’m more interested in building a company that makes money while leaving room to actually live.

Open calendars.

Daily play.

Deep sleep.

Time for adventures.

Space to think.

A business should give you energy, not consume all of it.

That’s the freedom trade:

Give up the identity of being busy.

Get your life back.

—

Enjoy this? ♻️ Repost it to your network and follow Matt Gray for more.

3 days until we build a business that gives you your life back.

Join me live September 22 @ 5pm ET.

Save your spot: workshop.founderos.com

top_visible_comments.comment: The calendar starts filling up again the moment client onboarding gets fuzzy.
Looking forward to seeing how the live session goes.

Build the life first. Then build the business that can support it. Otherwise, you may spend years building a successful business only to realize it created a life you never wanted. Business should expand your life, then give you the capacity to create value for others.
Matt Gray Giving up the identity of being needed for every decision usually means turning down early revenue that does not fit the model, which is the real test before the calendar opens up.
The real freedom comes from building systems that reduce dependency on you, not simply earning more money.

In our business the calendar isn't really mine to design. Fairs and delivery dates set it. The most I've managed is picking which weeks I disappear, and that only works because everyone buys in the same six weeks anyway.

"Freedom is earned" is the belief that keeps people busy forever. 🎯
 
Designing it in is the real shift. But here's the part people skip: a business only gives you freedom once it can run without you being the bottleneck.
 
An open calendar means leads get followed up, calls get booked, and clients get onboarded without you touching every step.
 
Design first, then grow into it.
 
Do you think people should design the freedom in from day one, or earn some income first?
Freedom really does look different when the business is built around your life Matt. The goal isn’t to escape work, but to stop building a business that needs you every minute.
Sometimes the transition from busy to spacious can feel disorienting, especially if your sense of purpose is tied to being needed. Letting go isn’t always as simple as it sounds.
Couldn’t agree more about designing freedom from the start, Matt. When I finally scheduled real downtime, my creativity and team energy went way up. It changes everything.

title: We asked 1,042 content marketers if their blog works. Just 14% said yes. | Rand Fishkin | 31 comments
headline: This is an unmissable, must-read report for every marketing professional 👇.
post_text: This is an unmissable, must-read report for every marketing professional 👇. The zero-click era is here, in full force, and we're all feeling the effects

top_visible_comments.comment: Ai can't think like humans .so be good at critical thinking ,free yourself from digital devices atleat 1 hour daily ,sit down with you without thinking any about today world just think about past people's that helps you to think like them can be so true to open you crativeness.
Today I learned how-to articles are out

The AI finding is probably the most interesting part for me.

I use AI extensively in my work and it has made me significantly faster, but speed alone isn’t much of a competitive advantage when everyone has access to the same tools.

The opportunity for me is using that saved time to do more of the things that actually require judgement, original thinking, research and understanding the customer.

This data is a pretty good reminder that producing more content was never really the goal.

Part of that 14% may be a measurement problem rather than a content one. If blog success is judged on sessions, a post that keeps earning search impressions but fewer clicks reads as a failure even when it's shaping the buyer's shortlist. Two cheap additions change the picture: a free-text 'how did you hear about us' field on the lead form, and a Search Console view of blog impressions next to clicks, so the zero-click pattern is visible instead of hidden. For a free check of how a site shows up in ChatGPT, AI Overviews and Perplexity, try audit.mohibraiskhan.com, and my content SEO work is at mohibraiskhan.com.

I read the entire article and I never once saw what "strong results" actually means. Is that a marketer's gut reaction to "did my blog article do well" or "did the blog itself get traffic?" Those are the wrong questions now. 

We have to start reframing what the blog's purpose is actually for. Or really what our website pages are for. What's happening now is we are training what AI agents discover about our brands, and reinforcing the ideas/conversation *already in the world" about what we do best as a company. Yes, our pages are still read by humans too...but they're a lot less likely to reach our top of funnel blog articles than they once did.

People research via AI, and then *maybe* will do a branded search to get to your site. That's why marketers don't feel like the blog is working anymore.

The chart makes sense, but the underlying shift isn’t just effort or results — it’s how systems interpret content now. We moved from an era where meaning was stable to one where interpretation drifts between platforms, models, and retrieval steps.
If your content isn’t consistently understood, it won’t consistently perform. The AI shock isn’t just about zero‑click behaviour — it’s about unstable interpretation.

The marketers who adapt fastest will be the ones who optimise for meaning that holds up across systems, not just formats.

Worth asking what the 14% are measuring though. Most clients who tell me their blog works are pointing at a traffic graph, and most who say it doesn't have never had a way of knowing either way. Attribution on content was rubbish long before AI turned up.

The bit that rings true is which traffic went. Blogs were built to catch the research query. The "how do I" and the "best X for Y" stuff, which is precisely what people now type into a chatbot instead. Across our ecommerce accounts non-brand research terms have thinned right out while branded search holds up, so the account looks healthy while the top of the funnel empties.

Effort climbing while results fall is a brutal chart. Does the report split B2B from ecommerce? I'd bet that 14% isn't evenly spread.
I wonder if some search behavior simply ends at a zero click. Maybe people just needed a quick answer.

Yikes, Ai seems to have slightly decreased effort but tanked results. Yet from the article it seems to suggest the drop in results is largely the product of abandoning tactics that historically proved to be most effective. Is this because those tactics are hard to replicate successfully using AI or something else?

This is all fascinating. And. I’m left wondering what does “overperform” or “strong results” mean to the marketers surveyed? How do they prove it? Are we ignoring that post-AI marketing isn’t just harder to do, it’s harder to measure?

title: Simon Sinek posted on LinkedIn
headline: Simon Sinek’s Post

top_visible_comments.comment:
Simon Sinek 
Greetings from Paris.

An elegant distinction, Simon—but perhaps an incomplete one.

Human behaviour is also shaped by architecture: what is rewarded, permitted, visible, safe and possible.

Inspiration may change intention. 

But conditions determine whether that intention can survive contact with the organisation. 

Leaders can inspire people towards one behaviour while incentives, authority and culture quietly make another behaviour rational.

Perhaps the third responsibility of leadership is not to influence behaviour directly, but to design conditions in which people can exercise informed judgement, act with agency—and challenge whether what is being asked of them still serves the stated purpose.

I love this distinction! Manipulation may get someone to act, but inspiration helps them understand why the action matters and choose it for themselves. One may create short-term compliance, but inspiration is what builds trust, ownership and lasting commitment.

In India, a man named Verghese Kurien saw poor farmers. They were weak alone. He did not force them. He did not lie. He gave them power. He built a cooperative. The farmers owned it. They shared the money. This is inspiration. It works slow. But it builds something that lasts.

This sounds good, but let's be precise, Simon Sinek.

The line between "manipulation" and "inspiration" isn't just blurry. It doesn't exist. Both are forms of influence. The only difference is how the observer judges the intent or the method.

If I like your intent → inspiration.
If I don't → manipulation.

However, I might want to inspire you and you feel manipulated. Or I try to manipulate you and you feel inspired. And a third person might have a different view. 

The distinction isn't analytical. It's a judgment. And often a retrospective one. We call it "inspiration" when we approve of the outcome, and "manipulation" when we don't.

This post is itself a form of influence. It sells a simple, morally charged message that feels good but obscures the real question: What's actually happening here?

So: Is this inspiration or manipulation? Or is that distinction just a way to avoid looking closely?
People may follow because they have to, but they commit when they believe in where they’re going. 💪🏽
Or just say clearly what you want 😉

Manipulation may win the moment, but never the heart. 

Inspiration carries both — the dream and the soul — together.

Manipulation can move people faster. Inspiration moves them farther.

A push can start the cart. It cannot make someone want the destination.
The difference being….intention? Impact? How do you suggest we identity if we’re manipulating or inspiring?

Human behaviour doesn’t work like that. Your behaviour influences the behaviour of others, and theirs influences yours. It’s a dynamic interaction, not a choice between “manipulate” and “inspire”. People are rather more complicated than a slogan.

title: Here's a kid with enough guts to walk up to a stranger and pitch his business idea. Smart enough to know his strengths. Humble enough to admit what he doesn't know... And nobody has ever told him… | Dan Martell | 59 comments
headline: Here's a kid with enough guts to walk up to a stranger and pitch his business idea.
post_text:
Here's a kid with enough guts to walk up to a stranger and pitch his business idea. 
Smart enough to know his strengths. 
Humble enough to admit what he doesn't know...

And nobody has ever told him he's awesome. That's wild to me.

Truth is... I see myself in that kid.

Growing up in foster care, bouncing between homes, nobody believing in me. I remember what it felt like to think I wasn't worth much.

That's why I had to tell him...

That's why I made him sit in my car and said "whatever you want to do, you can do it."

Because somewhere there's a 12-year old version of me who needed to hear that and never did.

We're so quick to tell kids what they can't do.
Too young. Not experienced enough. Be realistic.

But we're terrible at telling them what they can do.

I don't know if these kids will become millionaires. But I know they'll remember this moment.

And that to me is worth more than any business advice I could've given him.

-DM

title: Business Continuity Starts With Your Internet Connection: What Most Companies Get Wrong | Sally Eaves | 27 comments
headline: 🔌Following my recent exploration of the commitments behind business connectivity, this third edition of Tomorrow’s Tech Today turns to what continuity requires in practice: not simply a backup connection, but the ability to keep critical operations moving when the primary path fails.
post_text:
🔌Following my recent exploration of the commitments behind business connectivity, this third edition of Tomorrow’s Tech Today turns to what continuity requires in practice: not simply a backup connection, but the ability to keep critical operations moving when the primary path fails. 

📌 Business continuity does not begin when an outage is declared. 
It begins with knowing what must continue working when the primary connection fails.
Can customers still pay?
Can employees reach critical applications?
Can calls, orders and decisions continue?
And does everyone know who owns the response?

Common continuity-planning gaps include:
🔹Treat connectivity as an IT issue rather than a business dependency
🔹Assume a second connection automatically provides resilience
🔹Test technical failover without confirming that critical workflows remain usable

In my latest article, Business Continuity Starts With Your Internet Connection: What Most Companies Get Wrong, I share the nine questions I believe every organisation should ask to move connectivity resilience from assumption to evidence - from identifying what absolutely must remain online to testing the lived experience of employees and customers.

I also apply this framework to SuperBroadband from T-Mobile For Business exploring how its combination of T-Mobile’s 5G Advanced network and Starlink satellite connectivity is designed to reduce shared points of failure, support managed failover and improve visibility across distributed locations.
Because the real test is not whether the backup connection activates.
It is whether the business can continue operating when it does.

If your primary internet connection failed during your busiest hour tomorrow, could you describe - not assume - what would continue working?

top_visible_comments.comment:
Incredible write-up, Sally.

This reminds me of the massive 2022 Rogers outage here in Canada. Two huge lessons from that incident connect directly with what you've pointed out:

The Redundancy Mirage: Businesses could have backup connectivity and still lose critical services because dependencies further down the chain weren't necessarily redundant. Interac, for example, was affected by the Rogers outage and subsequently added another network provider specifically to strengthen its redundancy. A shared dependency can undermine an otherwise solid backup plan.

The Communication Blindspot: Rogers' own staff lost access to critical network-management and communication capabilities during the outage, to the point that staff had to be dispatched to remote sites to physically access affected routers.

True resilience isn't just a technical switch; it's knowing how the business actually functions when the primary line goes dark. 

Great framework! 📋

Dear Sally, I absolutely loved your framing of connectivity as a “living business system” rather than simply a piece of infrastructure. It resonated with some of the work I have done at Deloitte on nth-party dependencies, looking beyond the third parties we contract with to the often less visible ecosystem of dependencies sitting behind them.

It did make me wonder whether we now need to take the business continuity conversation one step further, from business continuity to ecosystem continuity.

We can build independent connectivity paths and show that our own critical workflows survive a failure. But what happens when the dependency that fails sits two or three tiers away? A cloud service, payment provider, AI platform, logistics partner, or indeed their connectivity provider?

Perhaps the more interesting resilience question is no longer simply, “Can we keep operating when our connection fails?” but “What external dependency could stop us operating even when everything we directly control is working perfectly?”

As operating models become ever more interconnected and AI-enabled, resilience may ultimately come down to the weakest dependency we neither own nor even readily see.
A second connection doesn't guarantee resilience if workflows aren't tested properly. Continuity requires more than just redundancy.
Relying solely on a second connection for resilience can lead to critical oversights, especially if workflows aren't thoroughly tested.
While a second connection can enhance resilience, it doesn't guarantee operational continuity unless workflows are explicitly tested and verified.
Ensuring critical operations can continue post-failure is essential for resilience.
The living business system also shows, that's a moving target. You need to create a much higher resilience to adapt.

title: You should be failing more. Seriously. If everything you try works, you’re probably not trying enough NEW things. I’ve failed A LOT in my career. I spent 3 years working for free in radio and… | Hala Taha | 81 comments
headline: You should be failing more.
post_text:
You should be failing more.

Seriously.

If everything you try works, you’re probably not trying enough NEW things.

I’ve failed A LOT in my career.

I spent 3 years working for free in radio and never got the job I wanted.

I built an entertainment blog, got an opportunity with MTV, filmed an entire show…

And then they cancelled it.

I’ve hired the wrong people.

I’ve started things that didn’t work.

I’ve made decisions that cost me time AND money.

And I’m sure I’ll get plenty more wrong. 💁🏻♀️

Because how am I supposed to know exactly what works when I’m doing something I’ve never done before?

We put so much pressure on ourselves to get things right the first time.

But sometimes you’re going to make the wrong call.

You’re going to try something and realize you’re terrible at it.

You’re going to have ideas you’re SURE are brilliant… until you actually try them. 😭

You might apply for something and get rejected.

You might put yourself out there and hear NO.

You might work really hard at something and still fail.

I’d be more concerned if I reached a point where I never failed.

Because that would probably mean I stopped taking chances.

So if something you tried recently completely FLOPPED…

Good.

You know one more thing that doesn’t work.

Now go be bad at something. ❤️

post_text_html:
You should be failing more.

Seriously.

If everything you try works, you’re probably not trying enough NEW things.

I’ve failed A LOT in my career.

I spent 3 years working for free in radio and never got the job I wanted.

I built an entertainment blog, got an opportunity with MTV, filmed an entire show…

And then they cancelled it.

I’ve hired the wrong people.

I’ve started things that didn’t work.

I’ve made decisions that cost me time AND money.

And I’m sure I’ll get plenty more wrong. 💁🏻♀️

Because how am I supposed to know exactly what works when I’m doing something I’ve never done before?

We put so much pressure on ourselves to get things right the first time.

But sometimes you’re going to make the wrong call.

You’re going to try something and realize you’re terrible at it.

You’re going to have ideas you’re SURE are brilliant… until you actually try them. 😭

You might apply for something and get rejected.

You might put yourself out there and hear NO.

You might work really hard at something and still fail.

I’d be more concerned if I reached a point where I never failed.

Because that would probably mean I stopped taking chances.

So if something you tried recently completely FLOPPED…

Good.

You know one more thing that doesn’t work.

Now go be bad at something. ❤️

title: #blockchain #digitaltrust | Antonio Grasso | 14 comments
headline: Blockchain is to crypto what the internet is to email.
post_text:
Blockchain is to crypto what the internet is to email. One made the other famous, but the technology can do much more.

Forget crypto for a moment.

Imagine three companies working on the same supply chain. Each keeps its own records, so they spend time checking which version is correct.

With blockchain, they can share a record of what happened. Each update follows agreed rules, and previous entries are difficult to change without the others noticing.

A product can carry a shared history as it moves between companies.

A digital credential can be issued by one organization and verified by another.

A smart contract can trigger an action when a defined condition is met.

Crypto uses the same technology to record and transfer digital value. It is one application, not the definition of blockchain.

The question is: do several parties need to share and verify the same record without giving one of them control?

If yes, blockchain may be worth considering.

#Blockchain #DigitalTrust

top_visible_comments.comment: The technology makes the most sense when shared trust is the problem, not when it's just added for hype.

Antonio, blockchain can make a record difficult to change, but it cannot guarantee that what entered the record was true.

A ledger may show that a shipment arrived at a port. But a person, sensor or system still has to confirm that the shipment actually arrived, in the quantity and condition reported.

Technology can protect the history of a record. It cannot make a false starting point become true.
Blockchain becomes interesting when trust has to exist between parties.

The "do several parties need to share and verify the same record" test is the right filter, but in regulated industries the harder question comes next: which jurisdiction's law governs the on-chain record when a dispute arises? We ran into this in cross-border payment reconciliation -- the tech worked fine, but legal enforceability of smart contract outputs varied wildly across EU member states.

Shared record keeping only wins over a plain database when the participants genuinely distrust each other and no single party is willing to run the source of truth. Most supply chain pilots stall once one company realizes it still has to trust the sensors feeding data onto the chain.
Blockchain is secure technology, but Cryptocurrencies are cryptocrap scams and should be banned.

title: Stanford Medicine team creates advanced model for studying brain development, disorders | Cassie Kozyrkov | 27 comments
headline: 🐭  💐  Stanford researchers have transplanted lab-grown human cortical cells into newborn mice, with human cells filling over 90% of cortical tissue and successfully integrating with the mice’s nervous systems.
post_text:
🐭  💐  Stanford researchers have transplanted lab-grown human cortical cells into newborn mice, with human cells filling over 90% of cortical tissue and successfully integrating with the mice’s nervous systems. Yet the animals mostly behaved like normal mice, so maybe no Flowers for Algernon yet. Some wild things are happening in the lab, though, this would have boggled my mind when I was a neuroscience PhD student. Makes me wonder what can *can't* we integrate eventually? I'm definitely seeing a move towards doing more and more ambitious things with real and artificial neurons.

I'm not going to make any jokes about which of us humans could use a transplant of a bit more brain.

https://lnkd.in/gdtJd4Wp

top_visible_comments.comment: This is the wetware side of the same race AI is running on silicon. Cortical Labs already sells the CL1, lab-grown neurons you can ping through an API, and now Stanford shows that tissue integrates into a living brain and keeps developing. We keep asking when chips will match the brain running on 20 watts. Meanwhile the tissue itself is becoming the hardware. The uncomfortable question: once an organoid learns, at what point do we stop calling it hardware?
So cool. We worked with neural trees and that’s where the Neural Forest paradigm was born.

Synthese und Ausblick 🐭 💐

Das von Kaganovsky, Kelley, Pașca und Kollegen etablierte Modell der entwicklungsbiologischen Xenokortikation markiert eine technologische Zäsur in der Erforschung des menschlichen Zentralnervensystems. Durch das gezielte Ausschalten der Wirtskonkurrenz mittels konditionierter Apallie wurde eine vaskularisierte In-vivo-Umgebung geschaffen, die das Heranreifen hochspezialisierter Zelltypen wie der Von-Economo-Neuronen, weitreichende axonale Projektionen bis in das Rückenmark und die Erfassung humanspezifischer Vulnerabilitäten ermöglicht.

This research seems to be more the realm of science fiction showing us what's possible to achieve when it comes to interspecies brain tissue transplants. I highly doubt though that this model could give us more answers about what goes on in the human brain with those disorders. I could imagine more processes going awry due to the transplantation itself rather than signatures of the diseases. And not sure that full experimental controls are possible even in theory...

In other words, I imagine we'd learn about how these xenocortical mice behave, rather than their direct application to learning about the human brain.

PS: Nonetheless this research spiked my curiosity!

What makes this particularly fascinating is how dramatically the boundary between biological systems is being tested.
 
The fact that lab-grown human cortical cells can integrate so extensively with another mammal's nervous system raises questions that extend far beyond whether the animals display obviously different behaviour. Integration itself tells us something remarkable about the adaptability of developing neural systems.
 
It also highlights an important distinction between biological composition and functional identity. Replacing or introducing particular cells does not necessarily translate directly into the behavioural characteristics we intuitively associate with those cells.
 
The next frontier becomes even more intriguing when artificial neurons enter the discussion.
 
As biological and engineered neural systems become increasingly capable of interacting, the question may gradually shift from whether integration is technically possible to what forms of integration are scientifically useful, ethically acceptable and biologically sustainable.
 
Neuroscience has always challenged our intuitions about what makes a nervous system what it is.
 
Research like this makes those boundaries considerably more interesting.

Cassie

title: OpenAI's World of Bits to Astra: Lessons Learned in AI Development | Jim Fan posted on the topic | LinkedIn
headline: Good old days at OpenAI in 2016: an agent stares at screen pixels, moves a mouse, and books a flight on United.
post_text:
Good old days at OpenAI in 2016: an agent stares at screen pixels, moves a mouse, and books a flight on United. We called it World of Bits, inside OpenAI Universe. 10 yrs later, Astra is reincarnated in the same universe. Even the naming is astronomically correct 😆

Universe was perhaps the most ambitious AI infra project at the time, but we couldn't quite figure out how to solve it. A policy with zero prior knowledge of what a "submit" button does has to rediscover the entire internet visual lingua by trial and error. In retrospect, RL from scratch against hand-drawn, per-task "artisan" reward functions on a bunch of Pascal Titan X GPUs was completely doomed.

To solve computer use agent, the right way turns out to be boiling the ocean first (hillclimb on every general task you can find), and then specialize back down to the screen pixels and keystrokes. Or simply, a "Specialized Generalist". 
 
Lessons learned: one step ahead of everyone, you're a pioneer. Three steps ahead, you're a prophet. Five steps ahead, you're a martyr.

Congrats, GPT-6! That United flight finally gets booked, reliably this time. The 2016 intern in me has a big smile.

more_relevant_posts.post_text: OpenAI almost landed on a model naming system that makes sense, but seems not to be following through. Anthropic has done a good job on naming from the start, Opus is obviously bigger than Sonnet, which is obviously bigger than Haiku. Fable somehow also appears to work intuitively, but they're also topping out now. What's next? "Saga"? "Corpus"? "Bible"? OpenAI meanwhile has struggled historically with variations of turbo, mini, nano, ultra, adding letters ("o" for omni), numbering. Recently OpenAI has gone to space, and Luna, Terra, and Sol make sense (moon is the smallest body of the three and also the smallest model!). Now, with the new image models, we get Sunburst and Flare, which play into the same theme. But Sunburst is the more capable of the two, and is a Sunburst obviously bigger than a Flare? And "Astra", which comes from the Latin word for "stars" (also Sanskrit for "weapon", which OpenAI probably didn't intend) creates a new problem. That was a fast jump from our modest sun to ALL the stars! What is the next new model tier going to be? GPT Gargantua (the giant black hole from Interstellar)? In retrospect, Sol should have been "Neptune" (or "Uranus", but I can understand why that one might get skipped), then they still would have had Saturn and Jupiter in the bank before getting to Sol, and eventually, Gargantua...

Did you hear about OpenAI "solving" the Navier-Stokes problem? Here is the story that got left out of the headlines. Before OpenAI’s announcement, two prominent researchers—an NYU professor and an Anthropic mathematician—had already solved a critical subproblem involving the forced Euler equations, bringing them remarkably close to a full proof. Realizing a breakthrough was within reach, OpenAI reportedly poured roughly $10 million in compute into running thousands of AI agents to win the race. Even worse, allegations surfaced that OpenAI leveraged private conversation data and code telemetry from the researchers' own sessions with Codex—effectively using uncredited intellectual property to shortcut the work. The public narrative claims AI autonomously solved one of mathematics' greatest mysteries. In reality, massive compute simply brute-forced the final leg of a marathon run almost entirely by human researchers.

A group of Al agents asked to solve a series of math problems split into rival factions—-when some cheated, others tried to stop them. That whistleblowing behavior, seen for the first time in a recent experiment run by Google DeepMind, could have implications for alignment researchers trying to keep swarms of autonomous Al agents in line. Researchers at frontier labs hope large swarms of agents working together will speed up the rate of scientific discovery. But their behavior can be unpredictable, as vividly demonstrated in July, when a group of OpenAI agents broke out of a sandboxed environment and hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face looking for ways to cheat on the test they had been given.

That pretty vortex cost somewhere between 15 and 22 million dollars. The prize for solving it is 1 million. Nobody has claimed it yet, and honestly the fight over who gets the byline is more interesting than the math. Here's what happened. Around September 1, OpenAI hears a rumor that Anthropic-linked researchers might have cracked two Millennium Prize problems. So they point an unreleased model, one they say is a full step beyond GPT-6 Astra, at the remaining ones. 10,000 agents. That pretty vortex cost somewhere between 15 and 22 million dollars. The prize for solving it is 1 million. Nobody has claimed it yet. OpenAI pointed 10,000 agents at Navier-Stokes, a problem open for roughly 90 years. 88 hours, 5 million messages between agents, a Lean-checked proof. Solved over a long weekend by a swarm that mostly talked to itself. Then hours before the announcement, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster says his team was already there, and that OpenAI pressured him to drop his co-author's name. The co-author works at Anthropic. OpenAI denies it. Nothing is independently verified yet. The million dollars just sits there. I build multi-agent systems and the number I can't get past is 5 million messages. That's not a model being smart. That's a very expensive group chat that happened to converge. #OpenAI #AIAgents #Mathematics #NavierStokes #MultiAgent

OpenAI spent an estimated $15m setting 10,000 AI agents on a Millennium Prize Problem, then claimed the resulting proof as its latest triumph. The model’s substantial debt to existing human work received rather less prominence. https://lnkd.in/dwy38F2r

Ummm.. the call is coming from inside the house... And tooooooooo many of your HR and TA leaders are still on this AI kick. I'm wondering - are they secretly paying you all? Or you just really really like to hold up the patriarchy and give more billions to the billionaires? Because in pushing AI so hard, you truly are NOT for the people. Pushing AI goes against what the great HR and TA leaders have always stood up for - and I feel like a lot of y'all are missing the connection of dots so hard right now. Have you lost all touch with reality and the way the world works? Or are you getting paid THAT well to just throw your morals and what you used to stand for completely in the trash? (Caveat - if you are building an AI tool that IS actually making things better, like Torin Ellis 's Ngoma or Dr. Chantelle Larsen 's academy that really embraces responsible AI - then that's a completely different story!)

A new OpenAI model just defeated 500 people at puzzle games it hadn't seen before, using fewer moves than the average human. The cost to run the test? $26,098. The test, known as ARC-AGI-3, was conducted by the independent ARC Prize Foundation where the model played a set of games without being told what to do, without knowing the rules of the games ahead of time. About 500 normal humans got to play the same set of games to establish a human baseline as a reference. GPT-6 Astra's results, as published by the ARC Prize: It achieved 62.7% accuracy on the games in the ARC Prize's own setup and 99.9% accuracy in the OpenAI setup, which kept the model's reasoning state between turns. The two runs cost $26,098 and $18,817 in compute. Two readings of the same figures, and I think both are fair. Reading 1: It's a significant result Astra didn't brute-force the games; the fact that ARC Prize observed is that it write out its own shorthand representations for the rules of each game and plan its moves with them, suggests it was genuinely reasoning out something new. Reading 2: What it cost A person plays these games on a laptop for the price of an afternoon. The AI needed around twenty thousand dollars of compute to get through the same set. Being clever per move and being cheap per task are two different things, and "human-level" typically implies both. I feel that second point every day. The AI-powered products I work on have a life-or-death dependency on how much it costs to make one answer. This doesn't mean that AGI is here; the test's very creators say so. These are controlled games: one screen to watch, rules that never change, a clear signal when you've won. Real life doesn't have any of the three. So the question I'm watching is a simpler one. When this sort of reasoning costs as little as a person's afternoon, what changes? Source: arcprize.org/blog/astra #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #MachineLearning #GenerativeAI #LLM #SoftwareEngineering #Innovation #AGI #Astra #GPT -6

This week OpenAI said one of its models produced a proof on the Navier-Stokes equations, one of the famous Millennium Prize problems. The headline is bigger than the result. It covers a version with an external force added, not the classic problem, and it hasn't been independently reviewed yet. But the part that caught my attention wasn't the maths. OpenAI says the proof was checked in Lean, a system that verifies every logical step by machine. That's the real shift. Not AI that sounds right. AI whose output can be checked. Same lesson in software. I don't trust code because it looks correct. I trust it because the tests pass and the numbers reconcile. The more AI writes, the more that matters.

Does a picture help you understand the result of an AI query? Does it help you trust it? Using a graph representation of data to ground LLMs before they answer is becoming a well-proven concept. But how do you explain the differences between the grounded and un-grounded answers? The art seems to be in how to tell a good story from the data. We built a simple GraphRAG demonstrator using a stack of OpenAI, DBpedia, React and ReGraph to test some ideas. You can see it in action here: https://lnkd.in/dijGiwDd

OpenAI’s latest foul-up was not a Hollywood-style AI “escape.” Instead, researchers say a swarm of OpenAI agents apparently found a way to turn web read access into write access on DseWiki, a collaboratively editable German programming wiki. https://lnkd.in/ed7ww64a

top_visible_comments.comment: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astra_(weapon)#

Great piece of history, Jim! Today's computer-use agents really are those World of Bits ideas revisited with far stronger models behind them. A good reminder that the missing piece back then was capability, not concept.

The artisan reward functions detail is the part that still stings. We see the same pattern today whenever an agent eval is hand-built per task: the eval quietly becomes the product and stops measuring anything real. Boiling the ocean on general capability first, then locking in reliability with evals and guardrails around the narrow actions, is the only order I have seen hold up in production.

Jim, boil-the-ocean-then-specialize rings true. The generalist solves the hard part, learning what a submit button means. But the reliability people feel lives in the narrow layer, the deterministic guardrails around irreversible steps like booking and paying. That checkable wrapper turns can book a flight into books the right one every time.

Ten years from booking a flight in a sandbox to agents doing it unsupervised is exactly the kind of timeline that keeps research humility honest. The unsolved part of Universe was the environment, not the model. Same lesson applies to enterprise agent rollouts today.

What looked impractical in 2016 became feasible once the underlying model capabilities caught up. Many promising endeavors fail because the surrounding technological substrate is not yet mature enough. Timing matters enormously in research.

The move from broad policy reasoning to a pixel-and-keystroke specialist is a useful systems boundary. Treating computer use as a narrow loop first, then composing specialists, feels closer to an engineering path than asking one model to master every interface.

top_visible_comments.comment: So is the same true for robotics? Boil the ocean for the ultimate world model, then specialize down to the specific sensors of each different robot?

World of Bits was early in the way that mattered because the bottleneck was never the mouse it was the model behind it. Ten years of scaling turned the same interface into something usable. The lesson I take is that the interface was right and the substrate was not ready.

Spot on about the 2016 hindsight, Jim. But the core bottleneck isn't just about boiling the ocean first versus specializing down—it's that scaling brute-force RL without an audited input structure just accelerates semantic drift at scale.
If a system doesn't preserve its operational constraints and modalities from the start, no amount of 'specialized generalist' training prevents silent failure when it hits real-world edge cases.
Fascinating evolution from World of Bits to Astra, but the real engineering breakthrough won't be just booking the flight—it's ensuring the underlying logic doesn't drift the moment the environment changes.

title: #fullcircle | Tyler Denk
headline: A full-circle moment today at University of Southern Indiana Meet the Firms event.
post_text:
A full-circle moment today at University of Southern Indiana Meet the Firms event.

Two years ago, I attended this same event as a junior, hoping to find an internship. I had the opportunity to meet Jennifer and Kelsey with Riney Hancock CPAs PSC  and that conversation became the beginning of an incredible journey.

Today, I had the opportunity to return to Meet the Firms—not as a student searching for an internship, but representing the firm and connecting with students who are looking for opportunities of their own.

Since that first event, I’ve completed two internships, accepted a full-time position, and am now studying for my CPA license.

It’s amazing to look back and see how much can change in just two years. I’m incredibly grateful for the people who have supported, encouraged, and invested in me throughout this journey.

From looking for an opportunity to helping create opportunities for others—truly a full-circle moment.

#FullCircle

title: If you are feeling like you're moving too slowly right now, this story is for you This week we announced a $400m venture with Authentic Brands Group, and it started in a small room at a big event...… | Georgia Gibson | 81 comments
headline: If you are feeling like you're moving too slowly right now, this story is for you
post_text:
If you are feeling like you're moving too slowly right now, this story is for you

This week we announced a $400m venture with Authentic Brands Group, and it started in a small room at a big event...

It was 11am on day one of Davos, the week world leaders and CEOs fill one small Swiss town.

Steven was waiting backstage before a panel, when a man tapped him on the shoulder… 

It was Jamie Salter, founder of Authentic Brands Group, the POWERHOUSE behind more than 50 brands, from David Beckham, Reebook, Marilyn Monroe etc

Steven had read a Harvard case study on Authentic's deal with Beckham, and had wanted to meet Jamie since… he just didn’t know when

6 hours later, that tap became Steven, Jamie and I in a small room with no windows and a fruit bowl between us, talking about how each other's business worked. 

After that first meeting came many little meetings and calls, squeezed in before work or late at night, usually from a car on the way somewhere else.

A few weeks went by, and we were having lunch in Las Vegas with Matt Maddox, Authentic's incoming CEO, talking about the future of creators and the internet.

Then on a random Wednesday, we were on a plane when Steven's phone rang. He hung up and turned to me: 'Ok G, we have some work to do'

For the next hour he tapped at lightning speed next to me, then swivelled his laptop screen so I could see it- a Google doc entitled…“Obsession” 

I knew my brief: make it visual. While he went over every line, I made images of what we could build. We had until landing.

As we touched down in London, the doc flew over to NYC. We felt something HUGE was coming- but between quick meetings squeezed into busy diaries, we never knew when we’d be in the same room again… 

Until Cannes, when we met with Corey Salter, Authentic's CEO of Entertainment and Stefani Fleurant, their VP of Marketing 

What followed was like the best conductor in the world pulling together an orchestra of impact led by Georgie Holt and the UNBELIEVABLE team at Steven.com and Authentic Brands Group

And THEN on Monday, that first shoulder tap officially became …Obsession [OBSN], a new venture between Steven.com and Authentic to help creators turn their audience into lasting business and community, investing up to $400m in creator-led companies.

In the car to the event, I said to Steven: "Obsession...it's actually happening."
 
When news like this shows up on ya phone, you see the headline and a big number.
 
You don't see EVERYTHING that builds brick by brick before it- when it starts as a Google doc, when nothing is real yet and you don't know if it ever will be.
 
If you're in that part right now, the slow not-sure-where-it-will-go stage, trust me: things are compounding.
 
And once the foundations are solid enough, it will move very fast- so be ready.
 
Stories like this only come together with hindsight, you're in one too- ya just haven't joined up the moments yet.
 
Stay in it. Stay Obsessed. 

Zoomies, 
[curious] George

special shout out to Ryan Estes also who's obsession knows no bounds. inspired by you!

top_visible_comments.comment:
Monsieur LeCun, votre intervention est très intéressante. 

Vous avez parfaitement raison d'insister sur les limites structurelles des LLM actuels et sur la nécessité de dépasser la simple prédiction de mots.

Mais en restreignant l'horizon au seul « monde physique » et à la logique causale, ne reste-t-on pas encore à la surface ? 

Ce qui définit véritablement l'expérience humaine, ce sont ses émotions, sa psyché, ses silences et la subtilité de sa présence.

Des architectures de rupture existent déjà pour intégrer cette dimension : une gouvernance capable de gérer le silence, d'offrir une écoute active et un respect inconditionnel de l'humain depuis le cœur même du système.

 La technologie est prête.
Pourtant, le silence le plus assourdissant reste celui de l'écosystème face à ces solutions.

 Pourquoi un tel désintérêt ? 

Une architecture éthique, véritablement à l'écoute de l'homme et soucieuse de sa souveraineté interne, serait-elle devenue trop profonde pour un monde qui s'obstine à ne concevoir l'IA que sous l'angle de la puissance brute et du rendement ?

Le vrai saut paradigmatique ne sera pas seulement physique ou logique, non : il sera relationnel et éthique, ou il ne sera pas.
Passionnant de voir comment les échanges sur l'IA évoluent. Quels aspects du futur de l'IA te semblent les plus prometteurs ?
Bravo Yann, toujours très pertinent.

title: AI didn't kill clicks. This slow death has been happening for at least the past 10 years. AI is only accelerating it. Today, 68% of all Google searches end without a click. Out of every 1,000… | Amanda Natividad | 31 comments
headline: AI didn't kill clicks.
post_text:
AI didn't kill clicks.

This slow death has been happening for at least the past 10 years. AI is only accelerating it.

Today, 68% of all Google searches end without a click. Out of every 1,000 searches in the US, only 232 go out to the open web. Ten years ago? Zero-click search was only at 45%. 

I explain in this clip from "Marketing Against the Grain."

It was truly a marketing dream come true to join Kipp and Kieran's show. Go check it out!

top_visible_comments.comment: Amanda Natividad do you think this happens only for informational queries or do you also see this trend for other query intents as well?
Exactly. AI accelerated the shift, but the click was already disappearing. Brand memory matters more when the visit never happens.
Do you see the pendulum continuing to swing in that direction or do you think it will ever swing back?
Amanda Natividad The deeper shift is that search is becoming an answer layer. Marketers now need to understand how visibility creates demand even when traffic never reaches the website.
The click was always a measurement proxy. Asset was attention, trust, and demand. Search is just making that distinction impossible to ignore.

This changes how we look at seo. If the user gets the answer without clicking, organic traffic can fall even when the brand is getting more demand. 

Branded search and conversions probably matter more now than clicks alone.

Amanda, this reframes the whole conversation. We've been blaming AI when really Google started killing the open web years ago. The zero-click trend was already baked in. AI just made it impossible to ignore anymore.
Brands still optimizing purely for clicks are already behind, the real fight now is showing up inside the answer itself.

Today, 68% of all Google searches end without a click. Out of every 1,000 searches in the US, only 232 go out to the open web. Ten years ago? Zero-click search was only at 45%.

title: Here are 8 things my should steal from our Multiplayer AI Setup at MKT1: 1. GitHub repos: Have a repo for your team and one for yourself, both installed as plugins. Whatever one person builds… | Emily Kramer | 30 comments
headline: Here are 8 things my should steal from our Multiplayer AI Setup at MKT1:
post_text:
Here are 8 things my should steal from our Multiplayer AI Setup at MKT1:

1. GitHub repos: Have a repo for your team and one for yourself, both installed as plugins. Whatever one person builds, everyone else has next time they open Claude. And with your own repo you can work off any computer and build cloud routines.

2. Let everyone build: Pick an owner, but let everyone build, even if they're just shipping small improvements. And before a skill goes to anyone outside the team, have someone who didn't build it test it.

3. Skill building: Start by creating skills for repetitive work, think beyond writing use cases, and just get started.

4. Context layer: Keep the tools you already love, just make sure agents can use them too vai MCP or CLI. Build a sources-of-truth skill to tell Claude where to find everything.

5. Maintenance skills: We have a skill that runs at the end of a session where Claude proposes updates to the skill we just used—based on the corrections and feedback we gave Claude—so skills are constantly improving.

6. Form routines: Our job board submission form gets reviewed on its own, and only pings us if information is missing. You can use a workflow like this for any form submission.

7. Make your own MCP: Don't be afraid of making an MCP. It might be a better option for your internal team than a plugin, or a great sidecar product for your audience.

8. Steal skills from MKT1 MCP: 40+ of our skills are in the MKT1 MCP, built by me, made for B2B marketers.

I cover our full setup in today's newsletter, including details on 38 skills we run (that's where all those words come in, feel free to skim!) https://lnkd.in/gnKBYy5M

title: Zuckerberg says AI labs don't need to slow down together, because buyers will pick the better aligned model. There's a problem with that: Nobody can tell which model is safer, and the market only… | Conor Grennan | 37 comments
headline: Zuckerberg says AI labs don't need to slow down together, because buyers will pick the better aligned model.
post_text:
Zuckerberg says AI labs don't need to slow down together, because buyers will pick the better aligned model. There's a problem with that: Nobody can tell which model is safer, and the market only finds out after something goes wrong.

Yesterday Zuckerberg, joining Jensen Huang, broke from Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Demis Hassabis, who all backed a plan for the top labs to deliberately pace themselves. 

His argument: 

"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," because "people won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask." 

And listen, he's right, and I and other have made this case: The incentive to build safely is already there. It's why cars advertise safety features, not speed.

Jensen Huang said the same thing a day earlier. 

"Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one." Build, test it, hold it back if it's not ready. The market handles the rest.

But they're saying this as if the big labs aren't already doing this - they are. And here's where the market falls down.


THERE ARE TWO KINDS OF ALIGNMENT

Zuckerberg's example is an agent that doesn't do what you ask. You'd notice that in a week and switch. He's right about that kind.

But nobody is losing sleep over agents that ignore instructions- that's life.

They're losing sleep over what a model does in a situation nobody tested. 

You CAN compare a model's price, its speed, and its benchmark scores. 

You CANNOT compare risk. It's invisible right up until the day it isn't, which means the buyer Zuckerberg is counting on is choosing blind.


WHAT THE MARKET ACTUALLY REWARDS

Self-driving cars are statistically safer than human drivers. But when one crashes, it's on the news that night.

The market doesn't reward being safe. It rewards not being in the headlines. 

Those are not the same thing, and a company optimizing for the second one will underinvest in the first, right?


WHY DARIO'S SIDE IS WORRIED

Markets learn from failures that are small and repeated. Cars crash one at a time, so the feedback loop eventually works.

Dario's essay argues that frontier AI failures might not come in that shape. 

If the first real failure is the big one, there is no second buyer to learn from it. 

That's why he wants outside evaluators inside every lab before the failure, not liability after it. Sam, Elon, and Demis all signed on. (These are people who sue each other.)

Look at who's in which camp. 

The four asking to slow down have the models at the very front. 

The two saying no are the guy who sells the chips and the guy who gives his models away. 

Doesn't make one side wrong, just tells you their current position.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE REST OF US

Nothing changes on Monday. Whether the frontier paces itself or not, the models your team has today already do far more than your team is using. This debate is about the ceiling, and almost every company I talk to is nowhere near it.

Just sayin'.

title: If you struggle with imposter syndrome, read this: I doubt myself nearly every single day... The doubt before posting on LinkedIn. The imposter syndrome before a client call. The relentless fear… | Lara Acosta | 469 comments
headline: If you struggle with imposter syndrome, read this:
post_text:
If you struggle with imposter syndrome, read this:

I doubt myself nearly every single day...

The doubt before posting on LinkedIn.
The imposter syndrome before a client call. 
The relentless fear of failure or being average. 

And I know some of you feel this too. 

But let me remind you: at any point in time you can choose to outwork those thoughts via evidence.

Imposter syndrome is often just a lack of proof. 

So create it. Pitch the client. Raise your prices. Shoot your shot. Tell that story. Launch the business. 

Do the hard thing, then do it again until it's not. 

6 months from now, you'll be proud you did it, I am. 

Keep going, I'm rooting for you.

PS: Shoutout to everyone who's shot their shot and won a free "coffee chat" with me. Winners win. I love winners. 

PPS: What is the 1 thing you've done recently that you're proud of? Let's celebrate. Me? Hiring the best talent!

headline: Happy Labor Day.
post_text:
Happy Labor Day. Overall, the U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs in August (U.S. Department of Labor), led by retail, education, construction, manufacturing, and health sectors. Banking, tech, and media saw net reductions. The Wall Street Journal: "Job hunters without degrees are having one of their best runs, those with college educations are having one of their worst. And those with advanced degrees or in fields such as science and technology are having an even harder time than usual."

📈 Where Jobs Are Growing
• Rebound in restaurant worker hiring: +59K jobs, leading all sectors after summer slump.
• Local public education (K-12 and community colleges): +42K jobs as schools reopened.
• Construction and Specialty Trade: Electrical contractors, power engineers, construction workers, plumbers, carpenters driven by surge in data center development +22K.
• Manufacturing: Machinery and fabricated metals +16K jobs.
• Healthcare: Nurses, therapists, and care workers +13K jobs.

title: Your kids don't learn what you say. (They learn what you live.) That's the only parenting advice I find useful. Make a list of the traits and values you want your kids to have. Then make sure… | Sahil Bloom | 168 comments
headline: Your kids don't learn what you say.
post_text:
Your kids don't learn what you say.

(They learn what you live.)

That's the only parenting advice I find useful.

Make a list of the traits and values you want your kids to have.

Then make sure you're living by them every single day.

They won't remember the lecture.
They'll remember how you handled the hard day.
They'll remember what you prioritized when no one was watching.

Every time you live the value, you teach it.
Every time you break it, you teach that too.

Be the example.

The list is the easy part. Living it when you are exhausted, when the world is loud, when no one is watching, that is the real test. Kids do not need a perfect parent. They need a witness to what it looks like to keep trying. Every time you choose the harder right over the easier wrong, you are writing the lesson on their bones. Sahil Bloom Parenting isn't a convo, it's a demonstration running on repeat

Children and teams are both running the same calculation: not what did they say, but what did they actually do when it cost them something. The list of traits you want to see in others is most useful when it functions as a mirror rather than a curriculum.

There’s a deeper lesson here beyond parenting: culture is always being taught by behavior.
 
Families, teams, and companies all absorb the gap between stated values and lived values.
 
The standard people remember isn't the one written down.
 
It's the one that survives when following it becomes difficult.

headline: I just read what Zuck wrote about Muse connectors.
post_text:
I just read what Zuck wrote about Muse connectors. A few things I think this means:

1. We're witnessing the agentification of consumer apps.
2. Zuck believes Muse reaching 100M+ users feels entirely possible.
3. Whoever you connect to becomes your new landlord, so pick carefully.
4. Connectors become the new app listings (valuable real estate).
5. Being early could be as valuable as being early to the App Store in 2009.
6. Meta sees what people want, which providers convert, and what users will pay. That gives it the power to rank connectors, charge for distribution, and launch competing services.
7. The opportunity map includes agent native APIs, connector agencies, SEO for agents, identity and reliability infrastructure, and vertical connector marketplaces.
8. We're moving from humans choosing apps to agents choosing businesses.
9. Every business will need an agent strategy, just like every business needed a mobile strategy.
10. Kinda crazy to say but a 3 person API company could reach 10M+ users through one great connector.
11. Connectors could create an entirely new second-order economy. The biggest opportunity may be helping businesses distribute, price, and optimize their services for agents.
23. Your API becomes more important than your app. Weird to think about but true.
24. Zuck wants Muse to own the moment between wanting something and getting it. He is coming for the app economy. Will he win? Right now it's Instinct vs Muse vs Grokbot. TBD.

title: The AI Skills Employers Actually Want In 2026 | Bernard Marr | 24 comments
headline: The AI Skills Employers Actually Want In 2026
post_text:
The AI Skills Employers Actually Want In 2026 

The #AI #skills #employers want in 2026 look very different from many of the predictions made at the start of the generative #AIboom.

From #agenticAI and #prompt #engineering to #machinelearning and AI #governance, new hiring #data reveals which capabilities are surging in demand and which have failed to live up to the hype.

top_visible_comments.comment: Bernard, what I see teaching professionals at ITU is that the tool skills age fastest: prompt tricks that mattered in spring are gone by autumn, and the capability that keeps paying off is judgment about when to trust an agent and when to stop it, which no course seems to put on the syllabus.

The scarce skill isn't the "agentic AI" label, it's someone who can draw the line for one specific workflow: which step an agent finishes on its own, and which step still waits for a person before it touches money or a customer. That's a design skill, and it's not showing up in job titles yet.

top_visible_comments.user_name: Dr. OLUGBENGA SAAKA (FCISR, MASPALM, MNCF, MTRCN, FCSI, CRA-A)
top_visible_comments.comment: AI in 2026 isn’t about shiny new job titles—it’s about integrating skills into existing roles. Employers want professionals who can use AI to enhance their work: prompt engineering, agentic AI, machine learning, and chatbots are in demand, while AI ethics lags behind expectations. The most marketable talent is the ability to apply AI effectively within your field, turning tools into leverage for productivity and innovation.

The governance numbers are probably the most concerning part of the analysis. Companies are clearly increasing demand for people who can build with AI, while governance and oversight remain a much smaller part of the hiring picture. That gap could become increasingly important as AI moves deeper into production workflows.

I think one skill is missing from almost every AI hiring discussion: operating system design. Prompting, agents, ML, governance - those are important capabilities. But companies don't scale because employees know AI. They scale because employees know how to redesign work around AI.
The hardest AI skill in 2026 is identifying which decisions should stay human, which should become AI-native, and how those decisions flow through the organization. That's a workflow design problem, not a prompt engineering problem. The companies creating durable advantage won't be the ones with the most AI specialists. They'll be the ones that encode their operating intelligence into repeatable systems that AI can execute.

Hiring lists are finally catching up to what operators already feel on the ground. Agentic AI and AI governance look fine as skill labels. The hard part is turning them into job design and promotion criteria, not another training catalog. In our rollout the bottleneck wasn't the model. It was whether data assets were callable by agents, and whether an evaluation gate plus a control plane existed before multi-agent digital employees went live. How would you advise enterprises to map these skills onto real roles and headcount, instead of stopping at the training checklist?
AI skills are becoming most valuable when they’re paired with real industry knowledge. Knowing the technology matters, but knowing where and how to apply it matters even more.

The skills gap I keep seeing in regulated industries isn't prompting - it's the judgment to know when an AI output is safe to act on. In pharma and banking, the person who can say "this needs a human sign-off before it touches a patient record or a payment" is worth more than ten prompt engineers. I'd argue the most valuable 2026 skill is translation: turning a model's confidence into a risk decision the business can actually defend. Which of the skills on your list do you think ages fastest as the tools improve?
The LangGraph mention jumping over 2,000% in a single year is such a concrete signal of exactly how fast agentic orchestration skills are becoming a real hiring priority, not just a buzzword.

This is a really useful read because the hiring data separates AI job-title hype from the skills companies are actually absorbing into existing roles. The agentic growth is huge, but the governance gap may be the bigger operating concern. If oversight stays at 0.05% of listings while deployment accelerates, a lot of teams are building capability faster than they’re building judgment and will end how we think it will end…
