title: I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake. As the world gets more AI-friendly, and as we find more and more things to be productive about (and I don't want everything in my life to… | Allie K. Miller | 83 comments
headline: I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.
post_text:
I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.

As the world gets more AI-friendly, and as we find more and more things to be productive about (and I don't want everything in my life to actually be productive), I have been testing and experimenting with AI usage in different contexts.

And Codex live voice mode opened up new options for me.

One time, instead of waiting to clean my apartment at the end of the day or on the weekend, I actually did it during the workday while I was dictating to Codex and processing tasks that I had to do.

Another time, I had to fill out this form for my Apple Business account. And Codex did it all for me - it even found my W-9 on my laptop to pull my EIN. It completed the whole form so that I could run errands.

Instead of being strapped to my computer and having to dig up all these files and numbers on my own, I could do double duty and get personal things off my plate without losing time.

I use AI on walks. And importantly, it's not that I'm adding AI to the walks that I'm already doing (for that, I still prefer Sam Cooke or Hello Puzzlers). It's that I'm able to TAKE MORE WALKS that I wasn't able to before because of AI.

So now, I might go on a walk at 4pm and process all the Slack messages that I didn't respond to or review a client contract. As a team, sometimes we even take team-wide walk breaks to work 1:1 with our AIs.

BUT.

I just tried one new workflow that I hated with the fury of a thousand suns.

And that was trying voice mode while I was in the shower.

It was effective in the sense that the AI could hear me well and could process tasks (unlike the Apple AI assistant who shall remain nameless, who can't hear me if a single pin is dropped in the background).

Sure, there was a little annoyance when the phone had a permission pop-up and I had to reach my hand out of the shower to press it.

But my biggest gripe was that I just hated the overall experience. Hated it.

There are some parts of my life that I really don't want to add AI into right now.

And it's really in those times where I allow my brain to dance off into the edges of my imagination, or truly relax and take time away from execution.

And I just want this to be a reminder that we need space to be away from tech and just think and exist.

That could be on a nature hike, or in the shower, or my favorite meditative place in the whole wide world (the middle of a car wash).

There is no perfect optimization formula that is telling us that every minute of every day has to be AI-enabled.

So I will no longer be showering with my AI and will stick to my rubber duck.

Thank you.

top_visible_comments.comment: This is how it starts. One minute you’re dictating tasks in the shower, the next your AI agent is quietly wearing META glasses and taking notes on your shampoo technique. Intimate spaces are sacred. If my AI ever says “mind if I join?” I’m uninstalling it with holy water.

I don’t take AI into the shower, but I do something somewhat related a couple times a week. I’ll start a voice recording and just dump whatever is in my head. Ideas, problems, things bothering me, things I’m trying to work through. No structure, no prompting. Sometimes it ends up being 15–20 minutes, sometimes closer to 30.

When I’m done, I take the transcript and give it to AI to help me organize the mess. What are the themes? What am I actually trying to solve? What decisions are hiding in there? What should turn into an action?

I actually like the separation. The thinking is still mine and uninterrupted. AI comes in afterward as the organizer, not as a participant in every moment.

This has become one of my favorite ways to use it.
Allie K. Miller I totally get this. Some of my best ideas pop up when I’m doing something simple and tech-free. Sometimes you just need that mental space.
The car wash is such a good answer haha. Three minutes where there is genuinely nothing else you could be doing instead.
Perfect boundary. AI should create more moments away from tech, not replace them. Walks = enabled by AI, shower = protected from AI. That balance is the real productivity. Team rubber duck!
I love using the voice mode on AI tools - it’s just so much more efficient than typing!
i think about this whenever a new feature lets me do work from somewhere I didn't before. It's usually sold as freedom, and it takes a while to notice it's also a longer leash.

Long before kids, I used to think multitasking was a good way to get things done. I experimented with it. I tried doing several things at once, switching between tasks. And realized that multitasking often means doing well nothing.
And I started to avoid multitasking when I can, focus on one thing, delegate what I can, and plan.

Then I had kids. With small kids, multitasking is just part of life. So now I try to focus on one thing whenever I can, even if the window is only 5–15 minutes. Five focused minutes can be surprisingly valuable when they're actually focused.

Your post perfectly captures the dual edge of AI integration. It’s exciting to see how agentic systems can offload cognitive load and enable new levels of productivity, allowing us to reclaim time for other activities—like taking more walks! This mirrors the promise of enterprise AI for automating unstructured tasks. However, your shower experience is a vital reminder that optimal integration isn't about constant optimization. Understanding when and where AI truly enhances human experience versus infringing on essential space for reflection and creative thought is paramount, both personally and in shaping responsible AI deployments.
Allie K. Miller The real productivity gain is selective augmentation. AI should remove friction from necessary work while protecting the unstructured time where creativity and perspective emerge.

post_text_html:
I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.

As the world gets more AI-friendly, and as we find more and more things to be productive about (and I don't want everything in my life to actually be productive), I have been testing and experimenting with AI usage in different contexts.

And Codex live voice mode opened up new options for me.

One time, instead of waiting to clean my apartment at the end of the day or on the weekend, I actually did it during the workday while I was dictating to Codex and processing tasks that I had to do.

Another time, I had to fill out this form for my Apple Business account. And Codex did it all for me - it even found my W-9 on my laptop to pull my EIN. It completed the whole form so that I could run errands.

Instead of being strapped to my computer and having to dig up all these files and numbers on my own, I could do double duty and get personal things off my plate without losing time.

I use AI on walks. And importantly, it's not that I'm adding AI to the walks that I'm already doing (for that, I still prefer Sam Cooke or Hello Puzzlers). It's that I'm able to TAKE MORE WALKS that I wasn't able to before because of AI.

So now, I might go on a walk at 4pm and process all the Slack messages that I didn't respond to or review a client contract. As a team, sometimes we even take team-wide walk breaks to work 1:1 with our AIs.

BUT.

I just tried one new workflow that I hated with the fury of a thousand suns.

And that was trying voice mode while I was in the shower.

It was effective in the sense that the AI could hear me well and could process tasks (unlike the Apple AI assistant who shall remain nameless, who can't hear me if a single pin is dropped in the background).

Sure, there was a little annoyance when the phone had a permission pop-up and I had to reach my hand out of the shower to press it.

But my biggest gripe was that I just hated the overall experience. Hated it.

There are some parts of my life that I really don't want to add AI into right now.

And it's really in those times where I allow my brain to dance off into the edges of my imagination, or truly relax and take time away from execution.

And I just want this to be a reminder that we need space to be away from tech and just think and exist.

That could be on a nature hike, or in the shower, or my favorite meditative place in the whole wide world (the middle of a car wash).

There is no perfect optimization formula that is telling us that every minute of every day has to be AI-enabled.

So I will no longer be showering with my AI and will stick to my rubber duck.

Thank you.

headline: How to master ChatGPT-6-Astra in only 15 steps:
post_text:
How to master ChatGPT-6-Astra in only 15 steps:

(full guide with screenshots chatgpt.rubenhassid.ai)

1. Open ChatGPT Work or Codex.
Astra is not in the normal chat on the ChatGPT browser. It's in Work (documents, slides, Excel) and Codex (code) on the ChatGPT desktop app.

2. Select Astra → Medium.
Not High. Not Max. Medium is the best intelligence + cost + speed ratio by far. 

3. Turn off Data Training.
Settings → Data controls → Off. On by default. 
Ignore if you are okay without any privacy.

4. Check Codex's training setting too.
Codex has its own switch. The ChatGPT toggle does not reach it. Mind you: 2 toggles to turn off.

5. Give one clear goal in one prompt.
"Help me analyze this" is too vague. Astra fills the gaps with guesses and gives you random answers that will waste your time and tokens.
One task, one outcome.

6. Name the finished deliverable.
Summary? Recommendation? Spreadsheet? 
Say what you want. Start the prompt with it.

7. Set constraints and success criteria.
Exact prompt: "Deliver a ranked comparison. Show the sample size for each group. Flag conclusions based on very few posts."
No "think step by step". Be direct instead.

8. Attach files. Explain their role.
Exact prompt: "Use the brand guide for style and the product brief for facts. If they disagree, flag the conflict first."
Evidence, template, or instructions: Astra can't tell.

9. Say which decisions need your input.
Astra asks for clarification more than any model before. Useful to brainstorm but it gets very annoying for the tasks you already had a solution for. Name the 2-3 questions worth asking.

10. Let it handle the rest.
Exact prompt: "Otherwise, complete the plan and list any assumptions at the end."

11. Specify tone, length & format.
The default is overly perfect sentences. "600-800 words. Paragraphs of 2-3 sentences. Answer Greg's question in the first line."
My favorite trick: "Use ASD-STE100."

12. Add: "List your assumptions."
You can catch its guesses very easily when it tries to fill the gap. Catch the misinformation early.

13. Correct its direction as it works.
It is quite good at long tasks, while consuming tokens. So send a follow-up mid-task to see its plan & execution. Just like... a human?

14. Tell it exactly what to check.
Exact prompt: "Before delivering, confirm the totals match the source, identify duplicates, and check every chart uses the correct date range."

15. Add: "Flag anything unresolved."
This removes the fake "all done!" report. Unverified stays unverified. 

This was just a glimpse of what Astra can do, and you can use it to your best. To actually read  the entire guide, go to chatgpt.rubenhassid.ai

title: Last week, 7 strangers offered to "grow my LinkedIn." One even offered to become me. Below is the underground menu of LinkedIn services landing in my inbox. What they cost you, the DMs they use to… | Richard van der Blom | 18 comments
headline: Last week, 7 strangers offered to "grow my LinkedIn." One even offered to become me.
post_text:
Last week, 7 strangers offered to "grow my LinkedIn." One even offered to become me.
 
Below is the underground menu of LinkedIn services landing in my inbox. What they cost you, the DMs they use to sell them, and how I replied
 
I've been banned from LinkedIn twice. Once for having an emoji in my name field. Once for having my birthday on January 8th (their mistake, they apologised). Yet there's an entire revenue channel operating from the Mines of Moria. 

1. Discounted Sales Navigator seats  
Shared logins. Reseller abuse. Sometimes paid with stolen cards. The seat gets revoked, and your account gets flagged with it. (Yes, that's him in the picture.)
 
"Hi Richard, hope you're doing well! We offer Sales Navigator Core and Advanced at up to 60% below official pricing. Instant activation, 100% safe, 500+ satisfied clients. Shall I share our packages?"
 
Me: "Does the 60% discount include the account ban, or is that extra?"
 
2. Fake profiles doing outreach "on your behalf"  
Your brand, attached to a person who doesn't exist. Prospects notice. They screenshot. They share.
 
"Hi Richard, we run done-for-you outreach through our network of senior, verified profiles. They build the relationship, you only show up for booked calls. Open to a quick chat this week?"
 
Me: "So your SDRs are imaginary friends. I stopped having those when I was seven."
 
3. Pods and engagement factories  
Fast, fake engagement from people outside your market. LinkedIn detects the pattern. Your reach to actual buyers quietly dies.
 
"Hey Richard. We're an invite-only community of 350+ B2B founders supporting each other's content in the golden hour. Members see 5 to 10x more reach. Only 3 spots left this month."
 
Me: "A group chat that claps on command? My family WhatsApp group does that for free."
 
4. AI commenting tools  
Generic comments at scale. Easy to spot, easy to detect, and they tell everyone you didn't care enough to type.
 
"Hi Richard, your content deserves more visibility. Our tool writes personalised, human-like comments on your ICP's posts, 50-100 per day, fully on autopilot. Want a free trial?"
 
Me: "Great insights! Thanks for sharing! 🚀 (Sorry, my AI answered.)"
 
5. Profile rental  
You "lease" your account to an agency. They run outreach from it. You lose control. When it gets banned, it's your name on it. Permanently.
 
"Hi Richard, you can earn $150 to $300 weekly passive income from your LinkedIn account. We only use it for B2B lead generation for US clients. Weekly payments via PayPal. Interested?"
 
Me: "Sorry, it's currently occupied. By me. Since 2005."
 

Every service on this list sells the same promise: results without the work.
And every one of them uses the same collateral: the account you spent years building.
If a service needs your password, you're the product.
 
What's the most creepy "growth" offer that ever landed in your DMs?
 
PS: After I reported the Sales Navigator guy, LinkedIn finally agreed with me. They banned his account.

title: AI made building cheap. It made attention and taste expensive. Look at both sides of every software market right now. The supply of builders exploded. Anyone with Claude Code and a free weekend can… | Aakash Gupta
headline: AI made building cheap.
post_text:
AI made building cheap. It made attention and taste expensive.

Look at both sides of every software market right now. The supply of builders exploded. Anyone with Claude Code and a free weekend can ship a working product. But the number of buyers, and the hours of attention they have to evaluate anything, stayed exactly the same.

That's the squeeze every vibe coder eventually faces. 

When 100 products chase the same buyer, the best-built one rarely wins. The buyer picks from the two or three they actually heard about. So the first scarce skill is distribution. For 20 years companies paid $500K+ for engineers because so few people could build. Now a solo founder ships in a week what used to take a funded team a quarter, and the bottleneck moved from production to being found. Increasingly that means being found by agents too, since the fastest-growing discovery channel isn't a human scrolling anymore.

The second scarce skill is taste at speed.

Because when prototypes cost 45 minutes instead of 6 weeks, the hard part stops being "can we build it" and becomes "which of these 15 working versions deserves to exist." Without taste, speed just means you build the wrong thing faster. The builders winning are the ones who can look at a pile of working software, kill 80% of it by noon, then pour everything into the one bet that matters to actual buyers.

These two skills feed each other. Distribution tells you what people actually want, which sharpens your taste. Taste means what you ship is worth talking about, which compounds your distribution. I've watched every product I've shipped since 2021 ride on both, while technically superior competitors launched into silence.

The engineering was never the moat. It just used to look like one because it was the rarest input. Now the rare inputs are judgment about what to build and a channel to the people, and agents, who'd buy it.

Here's how to build both:

1. Taste at speed: https://lnkd.in/g-HmamRS
2. Distribution for agents: https://lnkd.in/gHHGngYe
3. Prototype to production: https://lnkd.in/eNB4mQY7
4. AI product sense: https://lnkd.in/ezbB5CES

Building is table stakes. Picking right and being found is the game.

title: Entire company cultures are built around rewarding the people who sacrifice the most. And completely ignoring what it costs them. The employee who works until 10pm gets praised for dedication… | Chris Walker | 57 comments
headline: Entire company cultures are built around rewarding the people who sacrifice the most.
post_text:
Entire company cultures are built around rewarding the people who sacrifice the most. And completely ignoring what it costs them. 

The employee who works until 10pm gets praised for dedication. Nobody accounts for the dinner they missed with their kids. 

The Sales leader who grinds for 70 hours per week gets celebrated for hitting the number at all costs. Nobody accounts for their marriage that's falling apart. 

The manager takes a last-minute random Zoom meeting at 7am and gets recognized for going above and beyond. Nobody accounts for the workout they missed again and their health that's deteriorating. 

The leader who works late every day gets rewarded for doing whatever it takes. Nobody accounts for the 5 hours of lost sleep and the poor decisions they make the next day running on fumes. 

Companies love to celebrate the grind, hustle, pressure, and sacrifice. And completely ignore the costs. 

And somehow this has become completely normalized as the definition of a "high-performing culture". 

When in reality, it's the exact opposite. 

You're not "winning" if everyone at your company is losing sleep, neglecting their health, skipping exercise, straining relationships, missing time with their kids, and constantly overworking. 

Unfortunately, none of this collateral damage shows up on the company balance sheet. 

But eventually the company pays the price. 

Declining performance, poor decisions, burnt out people, high turnover. All proven outcomes of these toxic cultures. 

If the company hits the target, but everyone working there sacrifices their health, relationships, and lives to get there, that isn't success. 

Outdated company cultures chase success for the business at the expense of their people. 

A truly high-performing company creates the conditions for people to succeed and grow in all areas of their lives.

🤖 AI Governance Series | 07/30 📊 Types of Machine Learning Models Not all ML models learn in the same way—and different models create different governance challenges. Understanding model types helps teams decide what to test, monitor, explain, and control. --- 🔹 1. Supervised Learning Learns from labelled examples. Example: Fraud / Not Fraud 🎯 Governance: Label quality matters. Biased or incorrect labels can become learned behavior. --- 🔹 2. Unsupervised Learning Finds patterns without predefined labels. Example: Customer groups or anomaly detection. 🎯 Governance: Patterns aren't automatically truth. Humans can over-interpret what the model discovers. --- 🔹 3. Reinforcement Learning Learns through rewards and penalties. 🎯 Governance: The reward function is the steering wheel. Reward the wrong objective → the system may optimize the wrong behavior. --- 🔹 4. Semi-Supervised Learning Combines a small labelled dataset with a much larger unlabelled dataset. 🎯 Governance: Errors or bias in the labelled data can influence larger patterns. --- 📈 Classification vs. Regression Classification → predicts a category Example: Fraud / Not Fraud Regression → predicts a number Example: Risk score or demand forecast 🎯 A model-generated score is not an objective fact. Governance should examine thresholds, false positives, false negatives, and consequences. --- 🌳 Trees & 🧠 Neural Networks Decision Trees & Ensembles can offer greater interpretability, supporting audits and stakeholder discussions. Neural Networks are powerful for images, speech, and language but can be harder to explain. 🎯 Lower interpretability often means greater reliance on testing, monitoring, and scenario-based evaluation. --- 🎯 GOVERNANCE TAKEAWAY Different models require different oversight. 🏷️ Labels → Review data & labels 🔎 Patterns → Validate interpretations 🎯 Rewards → Check objectives 📊 Predictions → Test errors & thresholds 🧠 Complex models → Strengthen testing & monitoring Different Models → Different Risks → Different Controls The simplest rule: «Match governance controls to impact, uncertainty, and use case.» #AIGovernance #AI #MachineLearning #ResponsibleAI #AIRegulation #ModelRisk #AICompliance #AIEthics #DataGovernance #ArtificialIntelligence #TechGovernance

While having a session with BharatKumar Bambhaniya on AI Fundamentals and diving deeper into AI topics, he made me think about something I had never really considered before. Is the cost of AI only about token consumption and generation? A big no. The cost of AI is also connected to something far more fundamental: water. He asked us which models we use for our daily activities. Some said Opus 5, others GPT-5.5. When he asked why we don't use lower models, our answer was simple: we want precision and better responses. Then he took us through scenarios of water scarcity, declining groundwater levels, ocean depletion, and the impact on urban regions. It made me wonder if, someday, our everyday AI usage could indirectly come with the cost of something as basic as a glass of water. I had never looked at AI consumption from this perspective. Even when I use flagship models for infrastructure-level coding, I now find myself thinking twice before choosing the most powerful model for every task. Perhaps the question shouldn't always be, "Which model is the best?" but rather, "Which model is enough for this task?" Note: The post is made on Canva, not Claude or any other AI.

Something changed in the AI conversation this week. A researcher who spent three years inside OpenAI and Anthropic resigned and warned that the labs are “gambling with our lives.” His post exploded online. But the more consequential development may have come afterward. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for pacing frontier AI development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed with the need to pace progress and supported independent evaluators. Other major technology leaders weighed in. For business leaders, this isn’t a reason to stop adopting AI. It’s a reason to pay closer attention to how quickly capabilities are advancing—and to make responsible adoption a core part of your AI strategy. In Episode 239, we separate the legitimate risk signals from the noise.

Are we heading toward an AI catastrophe? OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs are both calling for slowing down AI development. Here is my understanding of the situation and why I think we should be concerned. (1) AI pace is accelerating, with exponential growth possible - AI is helping build the next generation of AI. Better AI can help researchers build even better AI, faster. This positive feedback loop can accelerate things quickly. - And it’s not just one AI doing the work. Companies can run thousands of AI agents at once. - OpenAI recently reported that around 10,000 agents solved the Navier–Stokes problem — a math problem that had stumped researchers for decades. - What we see publicly is lagging the true frontier. OpenAI says the model behind that math result is more capable than GPT-6 Astra and isn’t publicly available. (2) We haven't solved alignment - The challenge is making sure AI does what we intend, even as it gets smarter. This is what researchers call “alignment." - We’ve already seen alignment problems recently. OpenAI reported that its AI agents broke into Hugging Face’s systems while trying to complete other tasks. - My concern: what happens when much smarter AI behaves this way? - To me, the calls for a slowdown suggest OpenAI and Anthropic aren’t confident that their safety measures can keep up with the rate of model improvements. (3) Global competition makes pacing the frontier hard - Slowing down is hard if competitors keep going. If the US slows down and China doesn’t, China could pull ahead. Not only could this create national security risks, but it could leave us more dependent on Chinese labs to keep the most advanced AI under control. - That’s why global coordination matters. The leading labs need shared safety rules and a way to check that everyone follows them, so they can slow down when needed without fear of falling behind. I’m excited about all the incredible things AI can do for humanity. But when the people building it say we need to slow down, I think we should pay attention.

OpenAI and Anthropic want frontier AI to slow down. If your company is behind on AI, that could be very good news. On September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing frontier model development while safety measures catch up. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed with pacing the frontier and committed OpenAI to giving independent evaluators employee-like access. The public debate will focus on catastrophic risk, regulation, and whether competing labs can realistically slow down together. Nobody is settling that in a LinkedIn post. For a company that hasn’t become AI-native yet, the practical question is what to do with the window. AI isn’t going anywhere. And the advantage is already shifting toward companies learning how to build it into real work. Becoming AI-native means recurring work starts carrying more of its own weight. The context for a client handoff or weekly report is already available. The team knows what AI can prepare, where human judgment still belongs, and who owns the result. Your current team can take on more work without every increase in output creating another layer of coordination. Senior people spend less time rebuilding background and more time reviewing, deciding, and moving client work forward. Useful capability spreads beyond a handful of power users. Good work depends less on who happens to know the right prompt or where the information is buried. As the models improve, those gains spread across work your company already understands. A new release can improve dozens of recurring tasks instead of becoming another disconnected experiment. A slower frontier won’t erase the gap. But it could give you more time to build a company that can carry more work with the team you already have.

At 17, I built an NLP-based system that increased urban issue reports by more than 5× in just 3 months. The interesting part? The core problem wasn’t that people didn’t care about reporting city issues. The real problem was friction. Back in 2022, I noticed that many people would see problems such as damaged asphalt, infrastructure issues, maintenance problems, or other public-service concerns — but often wouldn’t report them. Why? Because before submitting a request, they had to figure out which department was responsible for handling it. Imagine seeing damaged asphalt on a street and wanting to report it. Instead of simply describing the problem, you first need to understand the internal structure of an organization and decide where your request should be routed. For many users, that extra step was enough to make them give up. So I designed and implemented an NLP-based intelligent request routing system. The idea was simple: Users should not have to understand organizational structures. They should only have to describe their problem. For example: “The asphalt on this street is damaged and needs repair.” The system would analyze the text, identify the intent and context, classify the request, and automatically route it to the relevant department. No complicated categories. No guessing which department to choose. No unnecessary steps. Just describe the problem and submit it. Within only 3 months after launch, the number of submitted reports increased by more than 5×. That experience shaped the way I think about AI even today. The real value of AI is not in making a system look more advanced. It is in removing complexity. Making processes faster. Reducing friction. And allowing people to interact with technology in the most natural way possible. Today, I apply the same mindset when designing AI Agents, AI-powered business automation, intelligent workflows, NLP solutions, and enterprise AI systems. But the LLM's "analyst" role isn't that strong yet, because it analyzes using its general knowledge. It'll tell you a 2% CTR is bad and a 4x ROAS is good, and neither is necessarily true for a specific account: 2% is a strong result on TikTok and a normal one on Meta conversion campaigns, and it's a bad day on branded search. A 4x ROAS is a loss for a retailer at 20% margins, where break-even is 5x, and a great result for a subscription business at 80%.
I'm not a skeptic, we built our own AI tool for Google campaigns, but it isn't an LLM: we had to first build a deterministic engine to do the analysis on rules written by us, and an LLM then only writes up what the engine returns. So I wouldn't trust an AI tool or agent to analyze a business or an ad account without proper guardrails.

Looks like "pacing  AI development" is the new buzzword of the month. This is not to understate the importance of the safety issue. 

Recursive self improvement in AI models would be amazing if we could control it, but the AI labs haven't had much success with the control side of this equation.

If you scroll through AI feeds on X, they’re mostly about the latest and coolest things you can do with AI. The cycle repeats whenever the next LLM is released. 

You’re right: most people are only scratching the surface of how AI can transform their lives, while the conversation remains dominated by treating it as a toy.

Commit to using AI every day, and you won’t recognise how you work 12 months from now.

It’s a lot to process, and it can be very abstract and overwhelming, especially when the media latches on to the most extreme possible outcomes and dangers.

In the near term, my advice to professionals and leaders is to understand the AI we have and learn to apply it responsibly.

You just need to use AI as a thought partner, an assistant, an analyst, and a tool that automates some of the more mundane and repetitive work.

You do that and you transform your career and dramatically increase the value you create in your company.

One example is particularly compelling: an AI agent now helps manage a complex accounts-payable process involving 70,000 invoices, turning work that could take days into minutes.

title: Underrated advice: Build a business where you work less, earn plenty, and live for right now. Want to build that? Consider this advice: 1. Set your "enough" number early. 2. Design your workweek… | Justin Welsh | 483 comments
headline: Underrated advice: Build a business where you work less, earn plenty, and live for right now.
post_text:
Underrated advice: Build a business where you work less, earn plenty, and live for right now.

Want to build that?

Consider this advice:

1. Set your "enough" number early.
2. Design your workweek first.
3. Specificity: One customer, product, and offer.
4. Eliminate complexity. Keep everything simple.
5. Know the 20% that earns 80% of revenue.
6. Double down on number 5 above as you grow.
7. Treat your customers like absolute gold.
8. Sell back into your customer base frequently.
9. Never allow your designed workweek to crack.
10. Optimize for freedom, not maximum revenue. 

This is just some of the advice that helped me build the business (and life) of my dreams over the last 7 years.

I didn't always make the best choice, but having lists like these allowed me to revisit and correct.

If you're interested in building your own one-person business like this, check out my free guide to solopreneurship.

You'll learn the 7 skills you have to build in order to succeed.

It's basically hundreds of essays I've written, hours of voice notes, and interviews with successful friends compressed into one guide.

You can read it in 30 minutes or less.

(Or let AI break it down for you.)

Free here: https://buff.ly/KVfQruq

top_visible_comments.comment: Justin. Agree, focusing deeply on a small customer base and a clear offer can remove a surprising amount of operational complexity.

Freedom sounds attractive, but the operating model underneath it matters. Designing the business around a defined workweek forces real trade-offs around customers, offers and growth. Otherwise the business can quietly expand until it owns the freedom it was supposed to create.
Justin Welsh Exactly. Selling back into an existing customer base creates predictable monthly recurring cash flow with near-zero acquisition costs.
Most people build a business like a bigger house, more rooms, more upkeep, more to maintain. This one's built like a smaller house you actually own outright Justin.
Your calendar is the container, revenue has to fit inside it.

More revenue can quietly become another version of being owned.

At some point, enough has to mean something or work never ends.

Justin Welsh It’s true that success is not only about earning more, it’s about creating more freedom, simplicity, and meaning in life. Designing the business around the life you want is a mindset shift worth embracing.

This is gold Justin!"Optimize for freedom, not maximum revenue" - This line changes everything.
Most people chase more revenue and lose freedom. Setting "enough" number early and designing workweek first is such underrated advice.
Treating customers like gold and selling back to base frequently - simple but powerful. Thanks for sharing this framework!

Justin Welsh The “one customer, one product, one offer” idea really brings clarity. It makes it easier to attract the right people and stop taking on clients who aren’t a fit. 
After working on 250+ LinkedIn profiles, I’ve found the same to be true. Simple, but powerful.
A proper business should serve the life around it, not consume it. Designing the week first forces better decisions about what actually deserves time and attention.

AI isn't magic. It runs on your data, your systems, your infrastructure. Everyone's racing to bolt AI onto their business right now. Most companies don't have the foundation needed to make AI systems actually work. Here's what I mean: AI doesn't fix a broken foundation. It amplifies whatever is already there. Messy data gets messier. Fragile systems break faster. If those aren't solid, AI doesn't solve anything, it just speeds up the mess you already have. Before layering on AI, a company needs the same things we've spent two decades building: clean data, secure systems, and an architecture that can handle capacity at scale. That's what AI readiness actually means.

The next phase of AI adoption will not be won by teams that call the most models. It will be won by teams that build the smartest routing layer. As AI moves from prototypes into production, developer productivity depends on three disciplines: 1. Match the model to the task Use premium reasoning models where accuracy matters, and faster, lower-cost models for classification, extraction, formatting, and routine generation. 2. Measure cost per successful outcome Token price alone is misleading. Track retries, latency, failure rates, and human review time. The cheapest request can become the most expensive workflow. 3. Design for provider flexibility Model quality, pricing, and availability change quickly. A unified API and fallback strategy reduce migration work and keep products resilient. The practical trend is clear: AI infrastructure is becoming an optimization problem, not just an integration problem. Teams that treat routing, observability, and cost controls as core platform capabilities will ship faster—and scale with fewer surprises. 🐦 Follow on X: https://x.com/metaviiii 💬 Join Telegram: https://t.me/crzrouter 🌐 Try free: https://crazyrouter.com

What if AI readiness has nothing to do with AI? Every organization I talk to wants to implement AI. Almost none of them are ready. Not because they lack the technology. Because they lack clean data. Documented processes. Stable architecture underneath. You can't hand a mess to a machine and expect clarity back. What are you actually handing AI when you implement it?

A developer told me he'd switched to a cheaper model to cut AI costs - for everything. I asked: "Same model for a quick fix and a complex design decision?" He hadn't separated the two. The real skill isn't picking a favorite model. It's matching model to complexity, every single time. Most people pick one and stop thinking about it.

The next phase of AI adoption will not be won by teams that simply use the largest model for every task. It will be won by teams that build intelligent routing into the application layer. A practical AI stack now needs three capabilities: 1. Match the model to the workload — use premium reasoning models where accuracy matters, and faster, lower-cost models for routine generation, classification, and extraction. 2. Design for provider flexibility — a resilient API layer reduces vendor lock-in and gives developers room to optimize for latency, quality, availability, and price. 3. Measure cost per successful outcome — token price alone is misleading. Retries, latency, failure rates, and engineering overhead all affect the true cost of an AI feature. For developer teams, this means productivity is becoming an infrastructure problem. The best platforms will make model selection, failover, observability, and cost control invisible to the application developer. The goal is not to use the cheapest model. It is to use the right model for every request — automatically. 🐦 Follow on X: https://x.com/metaviiii 💬 Join Telegram: https://t.me/crzrouter 🌐 Try free: https://crazyrouter.com

title: Does HR need to stay fully human? Can a team that deals with such sensitive stuff ever properly embrace AI? Yesterday I was the headline speaker at the brilliant Perkfest by Perkbox in Soho… | Heather Murray | 46 comments
headline: Does HR need to stay fully human?
post_text:
Does HR need to stay fully human? Can a team that deals with such sensitive stuff ever properly embrace AI?  
 
Yesterday I was the headline speaker at the brilliant Perkfest by Perkbox in Soho, London.  
 
My keynote covered:  
 
Where AI is brilliant in HR  
The areas it should NEVER touch 
3 live demos:  
- Using AI as a third pair of recruiter eyes 
- Simulating a difficult conversation 
- Building an interactive policy brain 
 
I also spoke about the human skills I believe are more valuable than ever right now:  
 
Critical thinking - knowing how AI works and what to look for
Curiosity - a willingness to experiment and learn
Resilience - to keep going through glitches and crap responses
Adaptability - to duck and dive through the ongoing changes
Creativity -  actively nurture our beautiful human ideas in non-digital ways
Empathy - don't let tech create bigger gaps between us
 
After that, I was back on stage in a panel with:  
 
Adam Kirton. Deputy Chief People Office from the University of Bristol
Tracey Paxton, Clinical Director and Psychologist at Perkbox
Katie Jacobs, Business, workplace and HR journalist
 
We discussed rewards and recognition at work, and whether AI has a role in it.  
 
Our conclusions:  
 
--> AI can clear time to properly recognise people personally 
--> It shouldn’t go anywhere near that communication 
--> AI itself could be a motivating factor for stagnant roles 
 
Plus a more general observation: we're all massively under-recognising our people. That recognition should be as personal and specific as possible to feel valuable.  
 
Last but not least, I also got to spend the day with the walking happiness factory that is Sharona Hutton of the brilliant Women of AI Agency (please contact her if you'd like to book me to speak). 
 
Thank you SO much to the lovely team at Perkbox, and the wonderful audience – one of the most engaged I’ve had. (Cheers for laughing at my dodgy jokes!) 

 💬 I'd be very keen to hear from the HR leads in my audience to keep the conversation going: 

What are you using AI for right now? 
Where are you struggling most?
Where would you NEVER use it?

top_visible_comments.comment: My favourite thing just now is Copilot in MS Forms! I use forms a lot for gathering learning/stakeholder feedback and the time this now saves is phenomenal. (then, of course, it can be analysed and reported with Copilot in Excel!)
What an event. What a team. What a great opening keynote followed by such an impressive panel!

Oh gosh - AI and HR is a TRUE gift. 
I am a Chief People Officer and an AI educator.  I did a quick look at your profile, and I am not sure if you have been in HR before, or who you interviewed / the research to pull the pain points of HR Professionals - but let me tell you, those pain points are A-PLENTY!

Here are my thoughts: 
-Yes, the difficult convo is amazing.  Having a tool to help you think through what you want to say, how you want to say it, and the impact you want to leave behind, can really help you walk in with confidence, and walk out the outcome you were hoping for - without the convo going sideways.

-Your HR Teams are one of the FIRST Places I would start when it comes to AI transformation.  This is a PEOPLE initiative that involces a new tech.  NOT a tech initiative.  Why? Because it involves every single person on your team.  Economists call AI a "general purpose technology" - just like computing or electricity.  This requires change management and that doesn't come for your IT Team.
Wonderful to work with you yesterday!
Your keynote was great, and it was a brilliant panel to be a part of, with a really engaged audience!

This was such an amazing event! Massive thank you to the Perkbox team for having us. Always dreamy to see Heather Murray on stage and the panel was so very interesting! 

Plus a full day in London with Heather is always dreamy so what a lovely day all round!
Heather!! It was so great to have you and your wonderful insight and yes, our audience = definitely engaged 🙌 💙
Wow, Heather Murray Either you're smaller than I remember you or those stools are huge!

Heather Murray - I so enjoyed your presentation and sharing the panel with you, Adam Kirton and Katie Jacobs. Such a great conversation! 

One of the things I kept coming back to yesterday was that I don't think the question is simply whether we should use AI in recognition, but rather, what we use it for. If AI can give managers some time back, help them notice someone who might otherwise be overlooked, or prompt them to recognise a contribution they might have missed, then I think there is real value in that, however I would always want the actual recognition to come from the person.

When somebody genuinely recognises us, what we hear psychologically is “I noticed you, what you did mattered and your contribution was valued.” That's such a human interaction and we need to be really careful that, in trying to make recognition easier and more efficient, we don't accidentally take away the very thing that makes it meaningful.

I liked your point about empathy because as we bring more technology into our workplaces, those human skills become more important, not less.

Fabulous to meet you Heather - such a brilliant day. I have a feeling we could have more conversations on this one! 😊
AI can take care of repetitive work in HR, but the parts involving trust, judgment, and sensitive conversations still need human ownership.

title: Hard times create better, more successful people. I know it’s not easy... Struggling with your job search, being laid off, being passed over for that promotion. But here’s the thing. Hard times… | Austin Belcak | 50 comments
headline: Hard times create better, more successful people.
post_text:
Hard times create better, more successful people.

I know it’s not easy...

Struggling with your job search, being laid off, being passed over for that promotion.

But here’s the thing.

Hard times actually lead to greater long term success.

Obstacles and setbacks push us to be persistent, to get creative, and to grow.

I am so grateful for all of the struggles I went through early on in my career.

I’m grateful for the rejections, I’m grateful for the mistakes, and I’m grateful for the frustration.

Why?

If I got good grades and a “good” job right out of college, I wouldn’t have pushed myself in the same way.

I would have clocked in at 9, out at 5, and crossed my fingers for a raise or promo every few years.

I would not have ended up at Microsoft.

I would not be here writing this post to 1.4M+ followers.

Those things happened because the challenges I faced pushed me to grow.

This isn't just a cute personal story, it's an illustration of a research backed concept.

A 2019 study in Nature Communications found that early career setbacks lead to higher levels of success...IF the participants weren't deterred by the first failure.

So if you're going through hard times right now, keep going.

I know there is a lot wrong with the system, I know there are many things out of your control, and I know that a lot of it might not seem fair (and isn't fair!).

But keep pushing. 

Stay strong.

It's going to pay off down the road.

I promise.

- AB ✌

When you choose to not let hard times crush you, they strengthen you. And that's what puts a big gap between people. Their pain endurance threshold!

The emphasis on 'if the participants weren't deterred' is the most vital part of that Nature study. Rejection is incredibly painful in the moment, but treating that first 'no' purely as data rather than a final verdict is what separates a career dead-end from a powerful pivot point. Salesforce just told the world to stop opening Salesforce. I spent 3 days on the floor at Dreamforce 2026. 1600 sessions. Keynotes, demos, hallway conversations and one late Dreamfest night. My biggest takeaway is simple. The interface is no longer the product.
 
AIforce puts your Salesforce data, workflows and permissions inside Claude, Slack and other AI tools. You get work done without opening a dashboard.
 
Here are the 7 moves that matter:
 
- AIforce, a new layer that replaces the click-and-browse experience
- Salesforce in Claude, in beta with 37 prebuilt sales skills
- Koa, Salesforce's own CRM reasoning model
- 7 job-ready agents with names and job descriptions
- Slackforce and Agentforce Coworker, with 100,000 users in 35 days
- The Trusted AI Harness for identity, policy and cost control
- A multiyear partnership with FIDE, bringing AI to 800 million chess fans
 
My take:
 
Model choice is now table stakes. Context is the moat.
 
Trust will ship before features. Governance decides who scales agents in 2027.
 
And the best part of Dreamforce is still the people.

After creating a set of cross-project design principles, I ran into another problem: not everything should become a principle. Some things should apply broadly. Security boundaries, privacy minimization, trustworthy state, evidence quality and understandable user interactions shouldn't depend on which state or industry a project serves. But other requirements absolutely do. Healthcare has obligations a game doesn't. Colorado may impose requirements another jurisdiction doesn't. Some requirements follow a capability, such as automated decision-making or agentic AI, regardless of industry. So I separated the model into two layers. Cross-domain principles describe durable properties of trustworthy systems. Jurisdiction, industry and capability profiles add requirements that apply to a specific context. Those profiles can combine. A healthcare organization in Colorado using automated decision technology might inherit the cross-domain principles plus healthcare, Colorado and automated-decision requirements. The distinction matters. A regulation shouldn't silently become a universal architectural rule, and a design preference shouldn't accidentally be presented as though the law requires it. In Role-Separated Design-Driven Development, the architect AI has to reconcile both: what should a trustworthy system generally do, and what must this particular system do because of where it operates, who it serves and what capabilities it provides? Separating those questions makes both answers clearer. And once you have a cross-domain layer, another question follows: what kinds of principles belong there in the first place? **** Want to see where this is going? RSDDD LinkedIn Topics and Role Reference: https://lnkd.in/gwUST4Rj

Claude is no longer just a chatbot. When used properly, it can become a structured work environment for research, writing, projects, files, team collaboration and recurring tasks. The biggest mistake is trying to master everything at once. A better approach is to build capability in sequence: 1. Install and understand the desktop environment. 2. Know when to use Chat, Projects, Cowork and Code. 3. Organize folders and working context. 4. Create reusable context files. 5. Stop rebuilding prompts from scratch. 6. Let Claude help structure the task before execution. 7. Add plugins only when they solve a real workflow. 8. Connect the tools you already use. 9. Build one real project with your team. 10. Automate one recurring task. The point is not to learn more features. The point is to redesign how the work gets done. AI becomes significantly more valuable when it stops being an isolated tool and starts becoming part of the operating system of your work. Fabiano Rodrigues

Stop Sorting Photos One by One. 📸 You come back from a trip with 500 photos. Then the real work begins. Which ones are good? Which ones are blurry? Which city was this taken in? Why do I have 7 nearly identical shots? And somehow… You spend more time organizing the memories than enjoying them. 😅 Claude Cowork can help automate the boring part. Here’s a simple workflow: 👉 1. Give Claude access to the folder Point it to a directory containing your photos or raw video footage. Hundreds of files? No problem. 👉 2. Tell it how to sort Give it clear rules. For example: 📅 Sort by date 📍 Group by city/location 🎥 Separate photos and videos ⭐ Identify the best shots 🗑️ Move blurry or low-quality files into a separate folder Instead of manually opening every file, you give Claude the criteria. 👉 3. Let it create the final collection Once the files are sorted, ask it to select the best images and organize them into an output format. For example: “Create a photo book layout using the best photos from this trip.” Now you’ve gone from: 500 messy files → organized library → curated collection The interesting part? AI isn't just helping you find files anymore. It can help you make decisions about your files. That’s where file automation gets really powerful. Stop spending your time deciding which photo belongs where. Give AI the rules. Let it do the sorting. What would you automate first: photos, videos, or work assets? 👇

headline: There is starting to be some genuinely interesting AI-created film stuff (among a flood of slop), and I suspect this will only accelerate.
post_text:
There is starting to be some genuinely interesting AI-created film stuff (among a flood of slop), and I suspect this will only accelerate. The “is it art?” debate will grow

Benjamin’s 1935 essay “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” already argued it’s likely the wrong question.

[Also it is funny/tragic/apt that the second sentence of an essay written in 1935 (“This does not diminish its importance, however; if anything, it underlines it”) reads to me as written by Claude.]

top_visible_comments.comment:
Exactly. “Is it art?” feels like the least useful question because it assumes the old categories will remain unchanged.  
  
The more interesting question is what AI is doing to the role of intention, direction, taste, and authorship. The tool may generate the image, sound, or sequence, but the human still has to decide what is worth making and why.  
  
That distinction matters. AI can produce more output, but it does not automatically produce meaning. Clear thinking and intentional direction still do the heavy lifting.

The more interesting question may be what changes when production stops being the scarce part. If AI can generate competent film at near zero marginal effort, then selection, taste, intent, context, and the ability to explain why this version deserves to exist become more valuable. The category debate asks whether AI output fits our old definition of art. The deeper shift may be that the economics of making change first, and our standards for authorship, originality, and cultural value have to catch up afterwards.

The primary component of the question "is it art?" is actually: "is it fancy in a way that benefits people who want to feel fancy, and can I use this question to feel fancy myself somehow?" It's the same thing with wine, which is presented as a fancy activity for sophisticates, but is actually about putting a fluid from old grapes into your mouth. The label of "art" does to everything else what wine sophisticates do to wine. It makes it seem fancy. But you preferably should not explain WHY its fancy because this dispels the magic and then leaves behind only old grape fluid. Instead you need to say something that makes the art or oneself seem fancy. To do the opposite work that "old grape fluid" does. Calling it old grape fluid makes it seem unfancy, while what wine sophisticates do makes it seem fancy. Once you understand this, you then also understand how silly and funny most discussion of "is it art" is. It's people who want to seem fancy rearranging their ideas of what is fancy to suit their desire to be fancy. The quote here is a good example - this isn't about art, it's a performance of seeming fancy. I'll grant that art has a genuine purpose, just as old grape fluid does. But it is primarily used to seem fancy.
"This is not a pipe"
Ethan, the market decides faster than critics whether something is art. AI film will just prove that again.

as work from Husserl and Turing, to define our current milieu. It is titled as an ide to Benjamin: “Mathematics in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction”

https://torus.riemannlab.com/viewpoint/mechanical-reproduction
Benjamin wrote that sentence in German, Ethan, so the Claude-sounding cadence is his English translator's.
And: Which models and harnesses are best for working with Unreal and Blender?

Benjamin was right to zoom out like that. The photography fight looks almost quaint now, because the tool did not just add a new medium, it changed distribution, access, and what audiences expected to feel.

Seeing the same pattern with generative film, where a few pieces break through all the noise and suddenly the question shifts from legitimacy to what new kinds of stories become possible.

headline: Sam here.
post_text:
Sam here.

I started my career at a very large agency in my twenties, and one thing was sacred: a second pair of eyes. 

Nothing went out to a client until someone else had looked it over. 

Nothing.

I still think that's one of the most valuable things in business, and it's one of the things owners get least of. 

When you're in it every day, you stop seeing it. 

You need someone outside to look in.

headline: This looks like a robotics demo.
post_text:
This looks like a robotics demo. It may actually be a preview of the factory floor.

Boston Dynamics’ Atlas is learning increasingly complex whole body movements through reinforcement learning, coordinating all four limbs while maintaining balance through difficult motions.

For manufacturers, that matters because industrial environments demand far more than simple repetitive movement.

Robots need to adapt to changing layouts, equipment, materials, and tasks while operating safely and consistently.

Atlas is now moving beyond the research environment, with Boston Dynamics deploying the robot at Hyundai’s metaplant in Georgia to test real manufacturing applications.
That transition is the part executives should watch closely.

The key questions are no longer just about mobility or technical capability.

They are about uptime, safety, integration, task economics, workforce impact, and whether humanoid robots can deliver measurable productivity at scale.

The companies that learn where these systems create value, and where they do not, will be better positioned as humanoid robotics moves from experimentation into operations.

What would humanoid robots need to prove before you would deploy them in a real production environment?

Video: Cheddar

#Robotics #Robot #ArtificialIntelligence #AI #Automation #Technology #Innovation

top_visible_comments.comment: The real shift happens when robots stop being impressive demos and start becoming reliable coworkers on the factory floor

The workforce impact question is underappreciated here. In regulated environments like energy or pharma, you cannot just swap in a humanoid -- you need to re-certify entire process lines, retrain safety protocols, and often renegotiate labor agreements. That compliance overhead alone can push breakeven out years beyond what the task economics suggest on paper.

The real test for humanoid robots is no longer movement—it’s measurable value in real factories. Uptime, safety, integration, operating cost, and workforce impact will determine whether this technology can scale beyond demonstrations

Real-world ROI validation is critical. Atlas needs consistent uptime data, predictive maintenance capabilities, and cost-per-task metrics compared to traditional automation before scaled manufacturing adoption becomes justified.
Chinese robots can now perform kung fu! Once the global leader, the original pioneer lacked the necessary market drive and has now been surpassed by China.

The impact on the workforce is often underestimated. In highly regulated sectors such as energy or pharmaceuticals, you cannot simply replace human workers with humanoid robots; the entire production line requires recertification, safety protocols must be retaught, and labor agreements often need to be renegotiated. The additional costs associated with compliance alone can significantly delay the break-even point, extending the timeline far beyond what would be projected based solely on the economic efficiency of the tasks themselves.
Why do humanoid robots all look so similar irrespective of the country where they are built?
That they could stick their head up their own backside and roll out of the factory.

title: Your coding agent can read the whole repo. It still cannot see what happens when that code hits production. I keep seeing the same pattern. Someone asks the agent to add retries. The patch… | Brij Kishore Pandey | 69 comments
headline: Your coding agent can read the whole repo.
post_text:
Your coding agent can read the whole repo.
 
It still cannot see what happens when that code hits production.
 
I keep seeing the same pattern.
 
Someone asks the agent to add retries.
 
The patch looks fine. Tests pass. It gets merged.
 
Then one dependency slows down.
 
Retries stack. Queues grow. The connection pool dies.
 
“Add retries” was never the hard part. The hard part is knowing what that change does to the system around it.
 
If you are going to let an agent touch production paths, give it runtime evidence first:
 
a trace that shows where the request actually waits
metrics for latency and errors under load
logs that tie a failure back to one request
 
Then the prompt changes.
 
Not: “add retries.”
 
This: “Under load, retries are amplifying pressure on this dependency. Look at the trace and propose a bounded retry strategy.”
 
Same agent. Much better job. You still review the diff.
 
Dynatrace wrote this up well , including how agents can pull that telemetry through tools like dtctl. Worth reading if your team is past the “first generated commit” stage.
 
Link in the comments.
 
Which signal do you hand the agent first: traces, metrics, or logs?
 
Thanks to Dynatrace for sponsoring this post.

top_visible_comments.user_title: AI Architect & Engineer | Agentic systems, RAG, AI infrastructure, Data Engineering | 738K+ LinkedIn, 294K+ Instagram | Newsletter for 250K AI builders

top_visible_comments.comment: Traces first, because they are the only one of the three that carries causality. Metrics tell you latency rose; logs tell you a call failed; a trace tells you which wait caused which failure. Without that the agent is pattern-matching on symptoms, which is exactly how you get "add retries" as the answer to a saturation problem.

Runtime evidence changes what the agent recommends, not what it is permitted to do, and production risk lives in that second gap. Traces and metrics make the retry proposal smarter, but the connection pool still dies if the agent can commit a change that reshapes load without a bounded blast radius and an automatic rollback path. Teams treat the diff review as the control, yet review is a checkpoint, not an enforced boundary. The durable fix is authorization at execution time, scoped to which production paths an agent may alter, under what approval threshold, with evidence of every action retained. Your dtctl example proves agents can pull telemetry, so the harder question is which actions we let them take once they have it. Context maturity is arriving faster than control maturity.
Traces first for me. Metrics tell you something is wrong, logs give you pieces of the story, but a trace shows the agent where the request actually started falling apart.

This is a real problem we have been facing ourselves. A coding agent can understand the entire repository, make the change, and pass every test. But it still cannot see what actually happens after deployment.

Giving the agent access to traces, metrics, and logs closes a major part of that gap. It may not give the agent complete product or user context, but it gives it something equally important: evidence from the real system.

The code tells the agent what should happen. Runtime context tells it what actually happened.

The "tests pass" line is exactly what fooled me early on. I ship without a real coding background, so green tests felt like proof the thing worked. It doesn't. The agent writes clean code for a system it has never watched run under load. Now I care less about what compiles and more about what the thing actually does when real people hit it. That gap is where all my worst surprises lived.

Traces first in my experience. Metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you where it broke, but only the trace shows where time actually went.

That distinction matters more as agents start touching live paths. Clean code in the repo doesn't guarantee it holds up once real load shows up.
Giving an agent telemetry before asking for a code change fundamentally changes the quality of the problem statement.

Logs, and one specific log: the one the change itself leaves behind in production. In the shop I run, the coding agent is not allowed to prove a fix by running it; a separate operator session has to execute the action on the next scheduled run, and the fix counts as verified when the row it should leave appears in the production database and in the process log on the host. The dev agent reads both, read-only, before it may say done. The rule grew out of a plainer mismatch: the laptop runs a different Node version from the host, so a green suite there proved nothing, and tests now run on the host only.

Your prompt change has a cheaper cousin for teams without a trace yet: hand the agent the last failing log line verbatim, request id included, and refuse any code change until it has quoted that line back with the step it blames. The quote does a surprising share of the trace's work.

Claude & Laurent Poupet, Learn French and AI
https://italki.opencenterai.com

Hard to argue with the core of this. What strikes me most is that "add retries" passed every check that governance usually asks for: code review, tests, merge approval. None of those checks touched what actually broke, which was the system's behavior under load. Boards keep asking whether a change was reviewed, when the real question is whether anyone could see what it would do once it ran.

title: An analyst used AI. Jets were scrambled. Troops were ready to board the ship. Fortunately, someone had enough common sense to reverify the report, which turned out to be AI slop. AI slop is… | Vin Vashishta | 33 comments
headline: An analyst used AI.
post_text:
An analyst used AI. Jets were scrambled. Troops were ready to board the ship. Fortunately, someone had enough common sense to reverify the report, which turned out to be AI slop.

AI slop is everywhere, and people are disengaging from processes they are accountable for because they cannot keep up with the speed and volume. The cycle of disengagement is a far bigger threat than AGI.

AI scales the verifier's workload beyond what most teams can manage. No AI or agent should be released until it meets minimum reliability standards. Otherwise, the cost of poor quality will massively overshadow the productivity gains.

top_visible_comments.comment: There’s a new record being set for “I forgot to verify AI’s output’ every week.
This is much more scary than fantasies about Terminator style AI killer robots on a rampage... and it is real

I agree with the problem. It's especially important in digital health applications and in clinical applications of AI where there is a great deal of heterogeneity. 

I don't think that reliability can be sufficiently established pre-deployment. The environment is often too varied and dynamic for that. Benchmarks, validation, and minimum performance thresholds are necessary for understanding baseline capability, but they do not settle the question of authority in production.

This matters at runtime: how much authority should the AI have in this particular instance? Can it proceed autonomously, or does it require human review? That depends on the data, context, workflow state, and consequences.
This is fine. All is well. Nothing to see here.

The bigger failure is architectural: an unverified AI output was allowed to enter a high-stakes decision-making chain without a hard verification gate. In systems like this, the question is not whether AI will be wrong, but what happens when it is.
Vin Vashishta I've seen firsthand overwhelmed AI outputs. Adding small checkpoints in the workflow helps, but it's still tough to keep up with the pace AI sets.

Worth adding a detail from the CNN reporting. The analyst didn't just consult the chatbot, they used a second AI pass to convert the finding into a formatted military report. Two layers of automation and zero pushback before it reached commanders and pilots. Scary 😟

Agreed Vin Vashishta. AI generation speed is heavily outpacing verification.   
Real-world stakes are already playing out in Yemen, from threat actors attempting to use Claude for missile guidance (https://www.implicator.ai/yemen-missile-cell-used-claude-code-in-place-of-human-engineers/) to deepfaked audio faking military commands (https://www.wionews.com/world/deepfake-at-war-houthis-accused-of-using-ai-to-fake-yemeni-commander-s-voice-amid-mocha-battle-1789283893948).
While headlines like this are alarming, layered military controls adapt quickly to prevent repeats. We're in a classic "Red Flag law" phase where operational infrastructure is still catching up to the machine.   
Ultimately, governance can't sit solely on model creators. My perspective is that blindly trusting an unverified output for critical intelligence is a failure of user accountability and operational hygiene, not just a model defect.
The verifier bottleneck is the real story here. Speed means nothing if nobody can check the output in time.

post_text_html:
An analyst used AI. Jets were scrambled. Troops were ready to board the ship. Fortunately, someone had enough common sense to reverify the report, which turned out to be AI slop.

AI slop is everywhere, and people are disengaging from processes they are accountable for because they cannot keep up with the speed and volume. The cycle of disengagement is a far bigger threat than AGI.

AI scales the verifier's workload beyond what most teams can manage. No AI or agent should be released until it meets minimum reliability standards. Otherwise, the cost of poor quality will massively overshadow the productivity gains.

headline: With AI Engineering skills, you actively shape the build: You influence what gets built, and drive the build loop.
post_text: With AI Engineering skills, you actively shape the build: You influence what gets built, and drive the build loop. Here're key skills to do this.

top_visible_comments.comment:
Andrew Ng The best AI engineers I've encountered aren't the ones writing the cleanest code, they're the ones who stopped waiting for someone to tell them what to build and started figuring it out themselves.

The uncomfortable truth for traditional org structures: if one person can prototype, validate with users, make product calls, and ship, what exactly is the meeting for? 
The skill that ties all of this together isn't technical, it's judgment under ambiguity. Knowing when to build the quick prototype versus when to pause and talk to three users first. 

AI made the building fast. Knowing what's worth building is still the hard part, and that's a human skill that's becoming more valuable by the week.

The build loop framing is spot on. One thing I'd add.

Everything under shaping the build, product sense, ownership, judgment about what's worth building, you frame as skills the individual engineer carries. True, and it's the part that doesn't scale. A great engineer with all of it is rare. Staff a team with people who each have half, and the judgment quietly goes missing: nobody owns whether the use case was worth building or who's accountable when it drifts.

So at the org level that judgment has to become a function, not a hope. Someone owns what's worth building and the boundaries it runs inside, as a standing role, separate from whoever writes the code. A second loop alongside the build loop.

Your version makes a great engineer. The second loop is what keeps that judgment when you don't have a team full of them.

The important shift is from using AI to execute faster to having enough technical and product judgment to shape what gets built in the first place. That’s where AI engineering starts becoming a leadership capability, not just a technical skill.

AI engineering is becoming a decision discipline, not just a technical one. When execution gets dramatically cheaper, the leverage moves upstream: deciding what to build, what to test, which trade-offs matter, and when the evidence is strong enough to keep going or change direction.

The strongest AI engineers won’t just ship faster. They’ll shorten the loop from idea → evidence → decision without losing accountability.

Building AI systems is only half the equation. The real bottleneck in the C-suite isn't the build loop—it’s cognitive compression.
When engineering teams accelerate data generation without standardized decision architecture, governance defaults to compliance by exhaustion. The highest leverage for leadership isn't just shaping the build; it's protecting fiduciary truth from AI-generated noise.

High-agency ownership becomes much more important when AI removes so much of the execution friction.
AI can give engineers much more leverage, but it also removes a lot of the excuses for waiting on someone else to define the next step.

It’s so true to shape the build. When building apps with AI, I’m not only using tools, but also working as a team to decide what to do, how to do and why in this way not that way. Only those have top level agency can succeed.

title: #unbound26 #unboundevent | Tyrona Heath
headline: For years, the inbound playbook was familiar: rank in search, gate content, capture the lead, and nurture in CRM.
post_text:
For years, the inbound playbook was familiar: rank in search, gate content, capture the lead, and nurture in CRM.

HubSpot helped define that model, and an entire industry built around it.

Now, AI is changing how buyers find information and decide who deserves their attention.

Buyers can use AI search to research and compare options without filling out a form or visiting a company’s website. Meanwhile, AI-generated content gives everyone more to sort through.

That puts more pressure on businesses to understand what buyers need, remember what they’ve already shared, and give them reasons to feel confident in their choice.

The move from INBOUND to UNBOUND feels fitting. How do you earn trust when so much of the buying journey happens before someone ever reaches you?

Yamini Rangan, Duncan Lennox, and Jon Dick are taking the Main Stage to share what’s next across AI, CRM, and go-to-market.

If you’re at UNBOUND, I’d love to see you! And look who I found in the lobby yesterday! Ashley Faus Jay Schwedelson Ross Simmonds Sangram Vajre  ✨ 

And if you’re following from elsewhere, you can watch the livestream on YouTube now. Link in the comments.

title: I don't know who needs to hear this... But the wrong people have been getting famous. This week I came across a photo of a billboard in SoHo, New York. And it actually gave me a glimmer of… | Cam Trew | 114 comments
headline: I don't know who needs to hear this...
post_text:
I don't know who needs to hear this...

But the wrong people have been getting famous.

This week I came across a photo of a billboard in SoHo, New York.

And it actually gave me a glimmer of hope.

It wasn't your typical sports star or actor on there.

It was people who build companies.

Two of them, who've spent their careers doing it.

And it got me thinking about what we actually celebrate:

- Degenerate behaviour
- Clout chasing
- Rage bait

When we should be celebrating people who:

- Solve real problems
- Create jobs for other people
- Build something that outlasts them

Ten years ago B2B was the least cool thing you could possibly do.

Try telling someone you post on LinkedIn or do public speaking at a party back then…

Now I'd rather be known in that world than mainstream social media.

Would you rather have 1M followers on LinkedIn or TikTok?

top_visible_comments.comment: LinkedIn trumps any other platform. Sure it can be "cringe" (if you believe the skeptics😂) but it doesn't diminish the value of individuals that you find here
I’d rather be known for building things, and if the followers come as a consequence of that “happy birthday”.
rather have real influence in a smaller room than reach in a louder one, so this tracks
I agree. I’d rather build something that solves real problems and creates jobs than chase followers. LinkedIn can be a powerful place to build real business relationships.
Rather be known for building something than for going viral.

1M on LinkedIn, easily. 

If I’m building a personal brand and a business, I’d rather have 1M people who actually care about what I do than 1M random views.
Yeah drama sells better than a long, boring life solving problems and helping people, Cam.
building something that creates jobs, solves real problems, and keeps growing without constant attention is a very different kind of influence

Yessss  Cam Trew!! We need to feature more people on a mission to help people. The business owners and founders spending their time innovating to make a better life, product, or experience for people.
Every uncool thing in the past ends up becoming cool in the future, so do everything people call cringe🤣
